# Nekko Agent documentation

> Every page of https://nekkoagent.com/docs in one file. Generated from the Markdown in https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent.

<!-- https://nekkoagent.com/docs -->

# Getting started

Nekko Agent is AI help on your computer, for coding and everyday work. It reads, edits, searches and runs things in your projects, using AI that runs on your own machine, an online service you already pay for, or both. It is free, open source and MIT licensed.

## Who we are

Nekko Agent is made by [Nekko Labs](https://nekkolabs.com). We develop it in the open on [GitHub](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent): the code, the plan and the task list are all public.

We care about three things:

- **Your computer, your choice.** You pick which AI runs, what it can touch and when it needs your approval. Work that uses only local models stays on your machine.
- **Honest software.** The app tells you what a model will cost, whether it will fit in memory and what it is about to do. These docs mark what is planned as planned.
- **Fast and calm.** The interface never waits on the agent, and responsiveness is measured on every change.

## What Nekko Agent does

- **Use AI on your computer or online.** Run models with the built-in engine, connect Ollama, LM Studio or vLLM, or sign in with a Claude or ChatGPT subscription. Mix them in one workspace.
- **Pick the right AI for each job.** Use a capable model for hard work and a small local one for simple tasks. Local models have no per-token bill.
- **Work in your real projects.** The agent reads, edits and runs code in the folders you add, with diffs to review, guardrails and an optional sandbox.
- **Automate repeat work.** Schedule tasks and save workflows, with retry limits and a visible history.
- **Take it with you.** Pair your phone to drive the agent on your computer from anywhere, end-to-end encrypted.
- **Plug it into your tools.** Use it from the terminal, or as an MCP server inside Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other agents.

## Install the app

The quickest way to start is the installer.

1. Download the installer for your computer from [nekkoagent.com](https://nekkoagent.com/#download) or the [latest GitHub release](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/releases/latest):
   - **Windows:** the `.exe` installer
   - **macOS (Apple silicon):** the `.dmg`
   - **Linux:** the `.AppImage`, or the `.deb` for Debian and Ubuntu
2. Run it. On macOS, drag Nekko Agent into Applications.
3. Open Nekko Agent, add a project folder and choose a model on the **Models** tab.

macOS builds are signed and notarized, so they open normally. If Windows shows an "unknown publisher" prompt for an unsigned build, choose **More info**, then **Run anyway**.

## Run it from source

Running from source gives you the newest code and is how you work on Nekko Agent itself. It takes four steps: install the prerequisites, clone the repo, install the dependencies, and run `npm run dev`.

### 1. Install the prerequisites

You need three tools. Check what you already have:

```bash
git --version
node --version
cargo --version
```

**Git.** Any recent version. Get it from [git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com/downloads), or on macOS run `xcode-select --install`.

**Node.js 22.12 or newer**, which includes npm. Install the LTS release from [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org), or use a version manager such as [nvm](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm) or [fnm](https://github.com/Schniz/fnm). The project uses npm workspaces, not pnpm or yarn.

**Rust**, through [rustup](https://rustup.rs). The engine daemon (`nekkod`) is written in Rust and `npm run dev` compiles it. You do not need to choose a version: the repo pins one in `rust-toolchain.toml` and rustup installs it on the first build.

```bash
# macOS and Linux
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
```

On Windows, download and run `rustup-init.exe` from [rustup.rs](https://rustup.rs).

Rust also needs a C and C++ toolchain on each platform:

| Platform | Install |
| --- | --- |
| Windows | Visual Studio Build Tools with the **Desktop development with C++** workload (rustup offers to install it) |
| macOS | Xcode Command Line Tools: `xcode-select --install` |
| Debian, Ubuntu | `sudo apt install build-essential pkg-config libssl-dev` |
| Fedora | `sudo dnf install gcc gcc-c++ make pkgconf-pkg-config openssl-devel` |

On Linux, the engine's model runtime needs the GCC 13 C++ runtime or newer (Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13 or later).

### 2. Clone the repo

```bash
git clone https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent
cd nekko-agent
```

### 3. Install the dependencies

```bash
npm install
```

### 4. Start the app

```bash
npm run dev
```

This builds the Rust engine daemon and the app, then opens the desktop app. The first run compiles the daemon in release mode and takes several minutes; later runs only rebuild what changed.

To stop it, press **Enter** or **q** (or Ctrl+C) in the terminal. The app quits normally and stops the engine and any model servers it started.

### Other ways to run it

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run web` | The same app in your browser at `http://localhost:1440` |
| `docker compose up` | The web edition inside Docker, with your workspaces mounted as volumes |
| `npm run build` | Build everything without launching |
| `npm test` | Run the tests in every workspace |

## Next steps

- Take the [walkthrough](https://nekkoagent.com/docs/walkthrough) for a tour of the app.
- Set up [local models](https://nekkoagent.com/docs/local-models) or [sign in with a subscription](https://nekkoagent.com/docs/subscriptions).
- [Pair your phone](https://nekkoagent.com/docs/remote) to use the agent away from your desk.
- Want to help build it? Read [Contributing](https://nekkoagent.com/docs/contributing) and the [architecture](https://nekkoagent.com/docs/architecture).

### Closing the desktop UI and notifications

Closing the desktop window hides it to the tray; the engine and running work remain alive. This is not Quit. **Quit Nekko Agent** stops the service and managed processes; **Stop Nekko service** stops the service while leaving the UI available. This does not promise execution during OS sleep, shutdown or logout.

**Settings > Notifications > Desktop notifications** is on by default. The desktop's main process listens independently of the page for completed replies, failures, questions and approvals. A user Stop is not a failure. Clicking a native notification restores the UI and opens the chat. Turn the toggle off to opt out; notices can include the chat title and question, error or approval text. Browser editions use browser notification permissions instead.

The 2026-10-13 batch is implemented and unit/fixture interaction tested, not yet landed. Image inspection and native toast delivery/click/permission testing remain pending. Known issue under review: the native listener currently also posts for a focused visible chat.

### Create an agent, media session or terminal

Hover anywhere on the left navigation panel to open it and see each destination's name. On macOS, **Nekko Agent → Settings…** (⌘,) opens Settings and **About Nekko Agent** shows the About page.

Hover over the sidebar **+** to choose **Agent**, **Create or Edit Photos and Videos** or **Terminal**. Moving away closes the menu after a short grace period. Terminal uses your default shell; choose its type in **Settings → Terminal → Default shell**, or leave **Auto-detect** selected. Create or Edit Photos and Videos opens an image session; video generation is not available.

### Approvals and delegated work

When a tool needs permission, its approval card appears in the chat window, not the separate wall composer. An unrelated tool finishing does not dismiss that request. Read the exact input before choosing Approve or Deny.

For an identified subagent, **Open ↗** beside its activity row opens the child chat using the existing workspace navigation. The chevron still expands task details separately. If the app cannot safely associate a delegation with one child (including older activity after a restart), use the Agent Monitor subagent list instead; the row does not guess which chat to open.

---

# Nekko Agent walkthrough

A guided tour of Nekko Agent, from install to your first agentic edit. Screenshots
are from the running app.

- [1. Install](#1-install)
- [2. Connect a model](#2-connect-a-model)
- [3. The unified chat](#3-the-unified-chat)

- [5. Guardrails & sandbox](#5-guardrails--sandbox)

---

## 1. Install

**Download a build** for your platform from the
[Releases page](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/releases/latest):

| Platform | Artifact |
| --- | --- |
| Windows | `NekkoAgent-<version>-x64.exe` (NSIS installer) |
| macOS | `NekkoAgent-<version>-arm64.dmg` (Apple Silicon) |
| Linux | `.AppImage` or `.deb` |

**Or run from source:**

```bash
git clone https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent
cd nekko-agent
npm install
npm run dev          # launches the desktop app
```

Nekko Agent stores everything locally (under your OS app-data dir): settings,
sessions, memory, and a usage log. No account, no telemetry.

---

## 2. Connect a model

Open the **Models** tab. This is where Nekko Agent differs from most tools, local
model servers are first-class, not an afterthought.

![Models tab](https://nekkoagent.com/docs/media/models.png)

- **Auto-discover local** probes `localhost:11434` (Ollama), `:1234` (LM Studio),
  and `:8000` (vLLM). Anything running is added with one click.
- Connected local servers and cloud providers are grouped, and the groups sit side
  by side when the window has room. The provider groups use the full window width,
  and each sits in a container with a faint border and tint in its colour (green
  for local, blue for cloud). A group is never split: when it has more cards than
  fit on a line, they wrap inside its own container.
- **Add provider** lets you configure a server manually, or add a cloud provider -
  Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (just paste the
  base URL + key).
- For **Ollama**, you can **pull** new models and **load / unload** them into memory
  right from the card.
- The **Token usage** panel charts input/output tokens over time and breaks them
  down per model and per provider.

> Tip: set a default provider + model in Settings so new chats start ready to go.

> Can't find a setting? Click the search icon at the right of the **Appearance** heading in Settings and type a word such as "prompt". A second after you stop typing (or straight away when you press Enter) the page scrolls to the first match and highlights it. Use the up/down arrows (or the arrow keys) to step through the rest, and the X or Esc to close the search.

### Example: connect an LM Studio server

1. In LM Studio, load a model and start its server (Developer → Start Server).
2. In Nekko Agent: **Add provider → LM Studio**, set the **Base URL** to your server,
   e.g. `http://10.5.0.2:1338` (you can paste just `host:port`, Nekko Agent appends
   `/v1` automatically). No API key needed.
3. **Test connection** → the model dropdown fills with whatever LM Studio is serving.
4. Pick the model in the chat header and go.

**Reasoning models** (Gemma, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-thinking, etc.) are first-class:
their chain-of-thought streams into a collapsible **Thinking** block above the
answer, so you see progress during long reasoning and the answer stays clean.

---

## 3. The unified chat

### Defaults for new agent windows

Choosing a model in a chat or in **Add window** remembers that model and its provider for the next agent window. Choosing **Auto** remembers Auto, not whichever model it resolves to. Browsing a provider or opening an existing chat does not change this default; existing chats keep their own model choices.

A successfully changed **Permissions** mode (Ask, Guardrails or YOLO) becomes the default for new chats. **Effort** is set per chat (a chat that never picked one follows the app default), and the saved **Execution** mode is reused through the existing setup flow. **Incognito** and **Offline** are different: they apply only to the chat where you enable them and are never turned on globally for new windows.

The **Mode** button opens the Mode panel. Saved modes run down its left side; the settings sit in three columns: **Environment** (run on your machine or in a Sandbox, and whether edits go to a separate worktree), **Model** (effort for this chat), **Privacy** (Incognito, internet access, folders, approvals, tools, MCP servers and connectors) and **Approach** (skills). Every setting has a line underneath saying what it does. **Tools**, **MCP servers**, **Connectors** and **Skills** open a list out the panel's side.

The **MCP servers** and **Connectors** lists switch each one on or off for this chat only. A server switched off here keeps running for your other chats, and a connector switched off here is simply not read for this chat's context. Neither list can turn on a server that is off in Settings or a service that is not connected; links at the bottom go to those pages. Sub-agents a chat starts inherit its effort, servers and connectors.

Click a saved mode to apply all of its settings to the chat at once. Change anything afterwards and the panel offers **Revert** or **Update** for that mode, or **Save mode** to keep the combination under a new name. Click the star beside a mode to start every new chat in it; click it again to go back to your last-used defaults. A mode also remembers the chat's effort, MCP servers and connectors. You start with four modes: *Everyday*, *Deep work*, *Private* and *Untrusted repo*. A mode never includes your folders, and applying one that runs in a Sandbox opens the Sandbox setup first.

Under **Approach**, **Skills** holds the work modes: *Default*, *Better review*, *Design* and *Best output*. Picking one changes how the agent works in that chat and brings the matching skills with it (for example Better review applies `/review`, `/security-review` and `/review-council`), so you don't have to remember or type them. A work mode applies to that chat only, costs more tokens and time than Default, and never changes Permissions, tools, Offline or Incognito. Rows marked *Coming soon* (model router, system prompt, memory) are not available yet.


A successfully completed reply should not retain a stale **Reply interrupted** warning. When the final transcript records successful completion, that terminal record takes precedence over missing older tool bookkeeping. Explicit interruption markers, provider failures, and intentional stops remain visible; the app does not rewrite your transcript to dismiss them.

The left navigation panel curves into its tails about 10px beyond the icon rows, with matching curves at both ends. Opening a wall window reveals the incoming window and slides existing windows aside, without a separate corner-resize animation. Reduced motion disables the wall transitions.

On the Agents wall, the agent, image, and terminal icons with small bottom-right **+** indicators create new windows. A subtle divider separates them from the **Focused** and **Dynamic** view modes. Dynamic uses a lightning bolt icon. For an even **Grid**, open **Settings > Command Center**, choose Grid under Wall layout, and set Grid rows and Grid columns (1 to 6 each). These dimensions are remembered when switching layouts. The existing **Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+1**, **2**, and **3** shortcuts still select Focused, Dynamic, and Grid respectively; saved Grid layouts reopen unchanged. In Focused view, **New agent** fades straight into the new chat's prompt; once you send your first message, the composer expands into the full chat. The Focused window's border is a quiet tint rather than a bright outline. The right-hand dock is headed **Monitors**. Inside a window header, the larger accent-colored **Focus** icon sits immediately beside Minimize and opens that window in Focused view. Minimize removes only the wall window, keeping the chat in the Agent panel. The left navigation keeps its position and tint, with broad curved wings above and below the destinations.

The **Chat** tab is the heart of the app. There are no separate "chat", "cowork",
and "code" modes, it's one thread. Ask a question, or hand off a task and let
Nekko Agent act on your machine through tools (read / write / edit files, glob, grep,
list dirs, run shell commands).

![Unified chat](https://nekkoagent.com/docs/media/chat.png)

- Pick the **provider and model** from the header dropdowns at any time.
- Assistant messages render **markdown and code**; every **tool call** the model
  makes shows up as a card so you can see exactly what it did.
- Streaming is live; hit **Stop** to abort a turn.
- **Tools** shows a friendly action label, the literal tool name and a full wrapping description. Search matches labels, names and descriptions. Use the checkboxes to enable tools; keyboard focus and Space activation are supported. The menu (in the agent window's footer) lists the agent's tools by category: File system, Shell & processes, Desktop, Online, Agent and MCP servers. Turn single tools or a whole group on or off for this chat.
- The **globe** beside it blocks the internet for this chat (local models only). Online tools (fetching pages, the browser), MCP servers, connectors and sub-agents are turned off; file, shell and desktop tools keep working. Shell commands are not network-sandboxed, so a command can still reach the network.
- In the model picker, a local model shows its short name with the file it lives in beneath.
- Answers to the agent's clarification questions stay visible in the chat as Q/A replies, including when reopening an existing conversation. Selected choices and your typed note remain visible; skipped questions say they were not answered. These reply rows do not create another prompt or offer edit/rewind actions.

**Keyboard shortcuts**: Nekko Agent has a command palette (think Cmd-K everywhere):

| Shortcut | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Ctrl/Cmd + K` | Open the command palette |
| `Ctrl/Cmd + N` | New chat |
| `Ctrl/Cmd + F` | Find in this chat |
| `Ctrl/Cmd + \` | Toggle the context panel |
| `Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + E` | Complete the focused agent chat |
| `Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + M` | Minimize the focused agent or terminal board window |
| `Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Delete` | Delete the focused chat or close its terminal, with confirmation |

![Command palette](https://nekkoagent.com/docs/media/command-palette.png)

**Find in this chat**: click the magnifier in the chat window's header (the first icon, left of Changes and Files), or press `Ctrl/Cmd + F`. A small bar opens at the top right of the conversation. Type a word or phrase and every place it appears is highlighted, with the one you are on in solid yellow and a count that always starts at **1 of 29** (the first match from the top). Matching is by whole word and ignores case, so `scroll` finds *Scroll* and *SCROLL* but not *scroller* or *autoscroll*. Use the up and down arrows (or **Enter** / **Shift+Enter**, or the arrow keys) to step through matches; they wrap around at the ends, and a match far up the conversation is brought into view. **Esc** or the **X** closes the bar and clears the highlights. It searches the message text you see, not tool steps, reasoning or link addresses. On the Agents wall each window has its own magnifier in its title bar, and the shortcut from the shared composer searches the window it is talking to.

**Copy and paste in a terminal.** Right-click a terminal for **Copy**, **Paste**, **Select all** and **Clear terminal**. On Windows and Linux the keys work the same way as in Windows Terminal and VS Code:

| Shortcut | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Ctrl + C` | Copy the selection; with nothing selected it interrupts the running program, as always |
| `Ctrl + Shift + C`, `Ctrl + Insert` | Copy the selection |
| `Ctrl + V`, `Ctrl + Shift + V`, `Shift + Insert` | Paste |

On macOS, `Cmd + C` and `Cmd + V` copy and paste, and `Ctrl + C` always interrupts. The read-only Agent commands log can be copied but not pasted into. **Clear terminal** clears the screen and scrollback in the window only; the shell keeps running.

---

### Add windows and read the dock

The Agents toolbar provides direct **New agent**, **New image session** and **New terminal** actions, with no ellipsis or overflow button. The empty wall can still open the full window picker. Its Chat, Media and Terminal categories remain horizontal; opening it does not change the wall layout.

Each repository heading in the Agent panel also has a **plus** button for a new agent chat and a **terminal** button for a new shell in that repository. These actions use the repository you clicked, not another selected or default folder. In Focused view, the new window becomes visible; other layout modes stay unchanged. On narrow screens, the agent list closes after successful creation so it does not cover the result. If a wall filter would hide the window, it switches to All. The controls wait for creation to finish before accepting another click for the same repository, and failures show an error you can act on and retry.

Utilization shows a Claude subscription account once when provider entries share the same token key, preferring the Anthropic entry. Independent accounts and API entries remain separate. In Budget, choose today, 1wk, 1m, 6m, 1y or all-time; the active range is tinted. Spend, tokens, top agent, local tokens, savings and compared model membership all follow that UTC range, not lifetime totals. See [usage limits and prices](https://nekkoagent.com/docs/usage-limits).

These 2026-10-13 changes are implemented and unit/fixture interaction tested. Matching captures exist, but image/motion inspection remains pending; earlier walkthrough pictures are not visual proof of this batch.

### Find a chat

The magnifier beside **+** at the top of the Agents panel opens a chat finder. It starts with your latest chats, newest first, each with how long ago it was used (days up to 30, then months). Type to filter by title, first prompt or latest reply; the search runs once you pause typing, or straight away with Enter or the Nekko button. Click a chat (or press Enter) to open it. **X** or Esc closes the finder. Incognito chats are never listed.

### Complete, minimize, and delete

Hover a window's lifecycle buttons to see the action and hotkey. Shortcuts target the window you are using, not every chat. The **X** in a chat window's top-right corner (and on its card) is **Complete**: it closes the window and keeps the chat under its group's **Show completed** control in the left Agent panel for 60 days, where you can read or restore it. Right-click a completed chat there for **Restore chat** or **Delete forever** without opening it. Completing never deletes; **Delete** is a separate trash action. Agents you have not touched for a month are completed for you the same way; change or turn this off under Settings → **Complete idle agents after** (1 week, 2 weeks, 1 month, 3 months or Never). Pinned, running, waiting and sub-agent chats are never completed automatically. **Minimize** removes only the board window: the item remains in the Agent panel, and a terminal keeps running. Terminals do not have completed history; **Close** ends their process.

Settings has **Show tips**, enabled by default. Your first successful completion highlights Show completed with a dismissible explanation. On a narrow screen, the existing agent list drawer opens automatically to reveal Show completed without taking focus. If you close it, the highlighted Agents button lets you return to the destination. Opening or closing the drawer does not dismiss the tip. Turning tips off does not disable deletion warnings. The in-app delete dialog offers **Skip future deletion confirmations**; only choose it if you want permanent deletions without another prompt. Re-enable **Confirm deletions** in Settings at any time. General chats no longer display a redundant missing-project label.

### A composer that follows your draft

In the Command Center, one docked composer targets the selected agent window.
Click another agent window to write in that chat's context, or use the dock picker
to move the composer above or below the wall.

The reply editor grows with new lines and wrapped text, then shrinks when you
delete them. In the bottom dock it grows upward, leaving the agent board above
it in its own scroll area. Once the draft reaches the height cap, only the editor
scrolls; the header, send controls, queued prompts, images and skill rows stay
inside the composer ring. A saved manual height remains a preferred minimum,
not a ceiling that prevents a longer draft from growing.

Drag the line above the composer to resize it. It snaps to two points: its
default size and full size. Release near either one and it lands exactly there.
Snapping back to the default clears the saved height. Double-click the line to
reset it any time.

### Continue after an interrupted tool

After Stop or an interrupted delegation, either type a follow-up or use Resume.
Both paths repair incomplete tool-result history before the next model request.
Saved real results are retained; missing results are marked interrupted rather
than silently rerunning the tool. A typed follow-up stays your own saved message.
While a reply is running, queue your follow-up or interrupt the current reply;
a second direct send is rejected without discarding the queue.

Delegation still waits synchronously for the child. Parent-callable child status
and cancellation while waiting are planned, not available through this repair.

### Follow delegated work without opening every detail

Delegation cards start collapsed, including while a child is working or returning
a large result. Their compact, plain-text activity sentence shares its status
with the plan's sub-agent list and the working-subagent indicator:

- **Working**: the child is thinking, writing or using a tool.
- **Waiting**: it needs an answer or approval, or is waiting to retry.
- **Completed**, **Failed** or **Stopped**: recorded terminal events, not guesses
  based on the presence of a stored reply.

Expand a card to read the full task and result in bounded scroll areas. This does
not resize the entire agent window. Summaries use existing local events, without
an extra model request or additional transmission.

Live card-to-child matching is best effort, using the parent, title and creation
time. There is no authoritative spawn-call child ID yet. Ambiguous matches and
historical calls without observed events do not borrow another child's status;
they retain a task summary or report that no current run status is recorded.

### Attach photos, videos and any file

The **+** button beside the message box opens a menu with an icon per row:
**Photo / Video**, **File**, **Folder** and **Skill**. Photo / Video follows the
model you picked: a model that takes images (Claude, GPT-4o and later, Gemini,
Llama vision, LLaVA, Qwen-VL and friends) gets the row enabled; a text-only model
greys it out and the menu says why, so a picture is never attached to a model that
cannot see it. Video input is rarer (Gemini, and OpenRouter models that list it);
when only photos are accepted the row says *photos only*. For a local model the
app cannot classify, the row stays enabled and the first send tells you.

You can also **paste** (Ctrl/⌘+V or right-click → Paste) or **drop** anything
onto the message box: a screenshot, a clip, a PDF, a Markdown file, a
spreadsheet, a file copied from Explorer or Finder. Photos and videos the model
can see travel with your message. Everything else becomes a file attachment: a
file copied from disk is attached in place, a pasted blob with no home (an image
copied from a browser, a PDF from an email) is saved under the app's data folder
first. Files whose bytes the model will not read (PDFs, Office documents,
archives, or a photo for a text-only model) still appear in the strip above the
message box, marked **name only**, so nothing disappears silently. Videos are
capped at 40 MB in the message; larger ones can still be attached as files.

### Diagrams, tables and code in replies

Replies render Markdown: tables, code blocks with a copy button, images, and
fenced ```` ```mermaid ```` diagrams drawn inline. Hover a diagram for **Copy**
(the Mermaid source) and **Expand**, which opens it in a full window where the
mouse wheel zooms, dragging pans, and a double-click resets; Escape or Close
returns to the chat. The assistant is asked to reach for a diagram when it
explains a flow or a structure, a table when it compares, and a code block for
anything you might copy.

### Photos from the web

When the agent finds a picture while searching or browsing ("what does the
HAMILeX MH-853 look like?"), it can show it in the reply. Several photos in a row
appear as a gallery. Photos load as you scroll to them, a few at a time.

Click a photo (or any image in the chat) to open the **photo viewer**: the
picture as large as the window, with **Copy**, **Save…** and **Close**, and for a
gallery the **‹ ›** buttons or the arrow keys to step through. Right-click a
photo for **Copy image**, **Save image…**, **Copy image address** and **Open
original in browser**.

How it stays safe: the chat never loads a web address itself. Nekko fetches the
picture for it, only from public websites (never this computer or your home
network), only real image files (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF) up to 10 MB, and
without your cookies or logins. A photo loads by itself only when its address came
from a search, a page or your own message in this chat. If the agent wrote an
address out of nowhere, the photo shows a **Load image** button naming the site
it would contact, so a made-up link cannot quietly send anything from your chat
to someone else's server.

### Plan and capacity at a glance

The plan icon in an agent window opens or closes only that chat's plan, sub-agents and queue panel. Each chat remembers its own choice locally. Narrow windows fold the panel automatically without changing that choice.

The context-window gauge has a subtle green background below 60% full, yellow from 60% to below 85%, and red at 85% or higher. Counts remain estimated; an unknown window limit stays neutral.

In Agents, the Hardware panel names each detected GPU and shows its own utilization. Missing readings say Unavailable rather than zero; switching monitoring off says Monitor off. VRAM remains the aggregate memory reading across devices. Where your machine reports them, CPU, Memory and each GPU row also show a temperature at the right of the label, orange from 80°C and red from 90°C. NVIDIA cards report theirs through their driver; Linux reads its hardware sensors; on Windows the CPU reading comes from the ACPI thermal zone, which many desktops do not publish, so it can be missing there.

**Using more than one screen.** In Dynamic view, the screens button at the right end of the wall toolbar shows how many screens are in use. Hover it to see your screens in a row: click one to open a full Nekko window on it (it swipes in from the left edge), click again to close it (it shrinks into the right edge). The main window's screen is always on. Each screen's window has its own left navigation, toolbar and wall, so one screen can show agents while another shows Settings. Under **View options**, choose **Prioritize empty windows** to send new agents to an empty screen first, or **Prioritize the main window** to keep new agents on the main screen. A window always keeps the agents you start from it, and your screens are reopened the next time you launch.

## 4. The Context Inspector

The right-hand panel (toggle it with the panel icon) is Nekko Agent's signature
feature. It shows **exactly what is entering the prompt this turn**, grouped by
where it came from:

- **Guidelines**: `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` / `.cursorrules` detected in your
  workspace folders
- **Files**: anything you've attached
- **Memory**: relevant global / per-project notes
- **Connectors**: issues, messages, or docs pulled in from Linear/Slack/etc.

Each item shows a **token estimate**, can be **toggled off** to exclude it, or
**pinned** to always include it. The bar at the top shows how much of the model's
context window you're using. No more guessing what the model "saw", you can see
and shape it.

---

## 5. Guardrails & sandbox

Open **Settings**. Two layers keep Nekko Agent from doing something you didn't intend.

![Guardrails & sandbox](https://nekkoagent.com/docs/media/guardrails.png)

**Sandbox mode** controls how the agent may touch your machine:

| Mode | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Workspace jail *(default)* | File access confined to your added folders; symlinks and junctions that point outside them are refused |
| Ask everything | Every write or command requires approval |
| Docker | Run shell commands inside a container if Docker is present |
| Off | No restrictions (power users) |

**Guardrails** classify risky shell commands and decide whether to **allow**, **ask**,
or **deny**, per rule, each toggleable. Ships with sensible defaults: recursive
force-delete, raw disk writes, `git push --force`, `curl | sh`, privilege
escalation, secret/`.env` access, and more. When a command matches an "ask" rule,
the chat shows an **approval bar** with the exact command and its severity before
anything runs.

---

## 6. Projects & the codebase index

The **Projects** tab manages your workspace folders, and yes, **multiple roots**
are supported. Each folder is indexed for files and code symbols (functions,
classes, interfaces, types) so the agent and search have a fast map of your code.

![Projects & index](https://nekkoagent.com/docs/media/projects.png)

- **Add** a folder and it indexes in the background.
- See **file + symbol counts** and index status per project.
- **Search** across the indexed files instantly, or browse the file list with
  per-file symbol counts.

---

## 7. Memory

The **Memory** tab is a simple, durable knowledge base stored as plain markdown.
Keep **global** memories (preferences, conventions) and **per-project** memories.
Relevant entries are surfaced in the Context Inspector and injected automatically,
so Nekko Agent remembers how you like to work across sessions.

---

## 8. Connectors

The **Connectors** tab links external sources so their content can be pulled into
context: **Linear**, **Slack**, **Discord** (token-based), and **Gmail** /
**Google Drive** (OAuth). Tokens are stored locally. Connect one, fetch a sample
to confirm it works, and the results become available to the assistant.

---

## 9. The mascot

**Nekko Agent** is the 8-bit cat that lives at the edge of the window. It waves to say
hello, peeks in from the side, and **"makes cat biscuits"** (kneads its paws) while
the model is thinking. Don't want it? Toggle it off in Settings → Appearance.

---

## 10. Appearance and page recovery

Nekko Agent starts in your system's light or dark mode. Leave the theme on
**System** in **Settings → Appearance** to follow system changes, or choose a
light or dark preset to keep that look. The pixel Nekko in the desktop's top
bar stays the same as you move between pages; the heading names the page.

If Settings or Nekko Server cannot load, the page shows the problem and a
**Try again** button. On desktop, start a stopped service from the tray menu,
then retry. In the web edition, check that the Nekko service is running.
Existing content stays visible when a refresh fails.

Agent shell commands are noninteractive: stdin closes immediately, so prompts
receive end-of-file rather than waiting for an answer. The shell tool has a
120-second execution limit and up to five seconds of stop cleanup; use
`start_process` for long-running jobs. On Windows, `date /t` displays the date;
bare `date` asks to change it. If a command appears stuck, Stop cancels its turn
and requests process-tree termination. An unresponsive OS process may still
need separate inspection even after the tool reports cancellation.

A failed chat reply preserves completed steps. **Retry** continues from saved
history, and you can send a new message instead. For Anthropic requests, Nekko
bounds supported outgoing image copies to 1568 pixels per side, including old
attachments and screenshot evidence. This prevents the stricter image-dimension
limit in requests with more than 20 images from trapping subsequent replies.
Saved originals are not resized or removed. Oversized animated images may be
sent as a static PNG. Corrupt or unsupported files, image-count limits, payload
size and context limits can still cause rejection; retrying those unchanged
inputs is not a guaranteed recovery. If such an error persists, use a new chat
with valid, smaller attachments and include the exact error in a bug report.

If a page or section cannot be displayed, use its **Try again** button to
reopen it. Navigation stays available so you can move to another page. If the
problem persists, include the displayed error and your app version and OS in
a GitHub issue.

---

Questions or ideas? Open an issue on
[GitHub](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/issues).

### Reordering project groups

Drag a project group header in the agent panel onto another group to place it before that group. A quick gap opens above the hovered group (beside it in the horizontal panel) and closes when you move away. You can drop on either the header or an agent card in that group. The project order is saved. Dragging an individual agent card still reorders or moves that agent, rather than the whole group.

### Agent window controls

Changes is the leftmost header control. When the agent edits files it uses a muted background without an outer glow and shows added/deleted line totals plus the changed-file count. Click it to review the diff. Zen focuses that window; a small divider separates this action from the Files, Browser and Logs panel buttons. The activity icon is at the top left before the numbered agent icon.

**Agent Monitor** opens the plan, sub-agents and queued prompts rail. Its control-panel button has a visible label and shows only while the rail is minimized; the conversation starts below it so it never covers your first message. With the rail open, the minimize button at the far right of its header puts it away again. Its **Project** group lists the work your project tracks: open items from a connected Linear, Jira, Asana, Trello, Todoist or ClickUp (one tab each), or, if none is connected, the unchecked items in the chat folder's `TASKS.md` (or `TODO.md`, `BACKLOG.md`, `ROADMAP.md`). Click an item to put it in the message box; nothing is sent until you send. The old header context button is removed; use Ctrl/Cmd+\ or the command palette's Toggle context panel command instead.

## Reports and artifacts in chat

Local document links in assistant replies appear as artifact cards beneath the response. The descriptive report title appears above its filename, so a README can still be recognizable. Select a card or document link to open it in the originating chat—not another chat that happens to have the file open.

Local SVG, PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP image markdown and image links also count as artifacts. Image markdown previews in the message; ordinary image links get a preview card below it. The same image does not get a second response card if it is already shown in image markdown. Cards fill the available width up to 768 px, contain images within 640 px height, and retain **Open source** to open the file in the originating chat. Local images load automatically outside Sandbox; unreadable, oversized or unsupported images show a fallback. SVG runs only as an inert image, with no scripts or external subresource requests. Web photos are shown through Nekko's safe fetch (see *Photos from the web*) and are not listed as artifacts; network shares and unsafe URL schemes are not previewed.

The desktop navigation rail stays 52px wide at rest. Hover a destination or Tab into it to reveal the labels in a 198px body; the extra 10px is right-side breathing room, not narrower buttons. Its subtle background extends equally above and below the menu along the left edge. At full available height, each straight shoulder runs from 40px wide at 95px beyond the nearest button to the 198px-wide body at that button, with slowly narrowing tails rather than curved, outward-flaring wings. Header clearance lets the upper tip extend beside the mascot. Short windows shorten both tails equally and keep the destinations scrollable. The decorative tails do not intercept clicks, and phones continue to use bottom navigation. Implementation is geometry-tested; matched visual and interaction verification is pending with the parent task.

The **Artifacts** tab on the left rail collects what agents made across all your chats: documents, web pages, designs, diagrams, images, data and office files, grouped by kind. Pick one to preview it, **Open file** to hand it to its usual app, or **Open chat** to see the chat it came from on the Agents wall in Focused view. Source code the agent edits is not listed.

At the top of **Agent Monitor**, expand **Artifacts** to see the session’s linked documents. It starts collapsed and always displays a count, including 0. A newly discovered artifact path expands just this section and highlights it with an accent border/background and a visible, screen-reader-announced **New artifact** status for ten seconds. Another new path restarts that deadline, including when one path replaces another without changing the count. The whole monitor never opens automatically. Initial history, switching chats and history loaded after a missing session do not trigger the highlight. Repeated links and previously seen paths do not retrigger it. You can collapse the section during the highlight; it stays collapsed until another new path arrives. When the highlight expires, the section keeps its current open or closed state. Non-image documents are not read until you open them; image cards load automatically when rendered. Host previews remain unavailable in Sandbox.

### Plan step status icons

In Agent Monitor, each active plan step has a static **Working** glyph and tooltip. Multiple steps can be working at once, even between streamed replies. If a reply was explicitly interrupted and no turn is running, active entries show pause bars labeled **Paused** until work resumes. Completed steps show a check, pending steps a hollow circle, and skipped steps a slashed circle with a struck-through title.

---

<!-- https://nekkoagent.com/docs/browser-automation -->

# Browser automation

## Dedicated browser

The desktop `browser` tool opens hidden, sandboxed Electron Chromium windows owned by the current chat, never your personal browser. Each chat has a separate in-memory session and up to eight tabs. Every browser action goes through Nekko's existing approval policy. Explicit visibility shows the owned window without activating it.

Navigate HTTP(S), inspect, click/fill the first match, type, press keys/chords, wait for content, scroll, extract text/links, evaluate page JavaScript, screenshot, manage tabs, read logs and take a snapshot.

A **snapshot** lists what the agent can act on: the page's links, buttons, fields and other interactive elements, one per line, each with a short ref such as `@e3`. The agent can then click `@e3` or fill `@e5` instead of guessing a CSS selector or writing a script to find the field. Pass a CSS selector to snapshot only part of the page. Refs belong to the page as it was; after the page changes, the agent takes a new snapshot. Approved screenshots go to the selected model. Evaluation runs in the page, not the app; pages can see text you enter.

Popups, downloads, JavaScript dialogs and device permissions are blocked. Local file navigation/uploads are blocked. Idle hidden sessions close after ten minutes. Requires a local desktop chat, not web/server/CLI or sandboxed execution.

## Native default (2026-10-17, release verification incomplete)

The default now uses pinned native Rust agent-browser 0.39.1 against Electron's existing Chromium. No extra browser download or global driver. Each adopted tab has a native process and a single-client authenticated loopback CDP relay restricted to its Electron debugger. There is no app-wide remote debugging port and no silent Playwright fallback. Missing native resources produce an explicit error.

The unmodified upstream Windows command daemon is unsafe for this boundary: it accepts unauthenticated TCP commands, and MCP stdio delegates to it. The user selected a maintained patch instead. Its only binary entrypoint uses inherited stdin/stdout, authenticates every command using a random capability delivered on inherited stdin, rejects all argv, clears upstream configuration and denies implicit browser launch and extra entrypoints. The CDP relay's distinct capability is also delivered privately on inherited stdin, not environment/argv.

Build the exact patch with `node scripts/build-agent-browser.mjs` (Rust toolchain and native linker required). Dist/release call this builder and package the native binary, license and pin outside asar. Source/dependency pinning is verified, not bit-identical output across toolchains. Windows x64 has been tested; installer/signing and macOS/Linux/arm64 remain unverified.

## Speed (2026-10-18)

A hidden window that has gone idle renders only about one frame a second, so clicks used to wait about a second and screenshots about two. The browser now keeps the hidden window's frames coming for just the duration of a click or screenshot; the window stays hidden. On a sample signup task (open the page, find the form, fill it, submit, check the result, take a screenshot) a new chat's browser finished in about half a second instead of about three and a third, on Windows. Opening the browser itself takes about 60 ms. A chat that keeps its browser open skips that and reuses the page cache. See [performance history](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/blob/main/docs/perf-history.md) and the [benchmark report](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/blob/main/reports/agent-browser/flow-benchmark.md).

## Checks and evidence

- `node --test scripts/agent-browser-native.test.mjs`: native framing/auth/argv/no-listener security.
- `node scripts/agent-browser-native-smoke.mjs [outDir]`: isolated hidden Electron native action/security fixture plus 20 cold-chat and 20 warm-inspect samples. Set `NEKKO_SMOKE_ELECTRON` to a matching owned Electron executable when needed.
- `apps/desktop/src/main/agentNativeRelay.test.ts`: wrong/missing auth, Origin, second-client and owned-target negative checks.
- `apps/desktop/src/main/agentCdpTransport.test.ts`, `agentBrowserActions.test.ts`, `agentBrowser.test.ts`: transport/page/bridge behavior.
- `node scripts/agent-browser-flow-benchmark.mjs [out.json] [--rounds 20] [--launches 12] [--drivers native,native-nowake,playwright]`: whole-task benchmark (navigate, locate, fill, submit, verify, screenshot) through the real bridge in hidden Electron, with first-in-process, fresh-chat and warm-session scenarios, tool calls, retries, reply bytes and startup phase timings. A `-nowake` driver runs without the hidden-frame wake.
- `scripts/agent-browser-benchmark.mjs`: explicit Playwright baseline-only helper; not the production default.
- `scripts/perf/lib/browser.mjs`: existing separate renderer-performance helper, not yet migrated by this task.

Full workspace typecheck/build and all 1362 desktop tests pass. Native fixture covers four wait states, duplicate-selector first match, keyboard submission, extraction, logs/page errors, tabs and popup/dialog/permission/file-navigation boundaries. Matching screenshot dimensions are 1359x873; parent actual-pixel review and public evidence publication are pending. All 956 host tests pass with explicit worktree-owned debug daemon (1 skipped); Rust browser/capture golden parity passes. Alternating benchmarks include native-child memory: cold navigation is slower, warm inspect slightly slower, working-set snapshots lower. This is a trade-off, not a speedup. Unpacked Windows native binary/license/pin hashes match staging; full signed installer and unrelated daemon resource staging remain unverified. See [performance history](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/blob/main/docs/perf-history.md), [raw baseline](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/blob/main/reports/agent-browser/playwright-baseline.json), [initial candidate](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/blob/main/reports/agent-browser/native-candidate-v2.json), [patch documentation](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/blob/main/vendor/agent-browser/README.md) and [original feasibility](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/blob/main/reports/agent-browser/feasibility.md).

---

<!-- https://nekkoagent.com/docs/local-models -->

# Running models locally

Nekko Agent runs models two ways: with its **own engine**, which needs nothing else
installed, or by driving a server you already run (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM). Either way
it loads a model with the settings you choose and tells you honestly whether it will fit
before you wait through the load. This is what the Models page shows you and why.

## The Nekko engine

The engine is llama.cpp, managed by Nekko Agent. You press one button, a build comes down
from llama.cpp's own releases (about 30 MB for Vulkan or CPU, several hundred MB for
CUDA), and the app can serve models. Nothing
is downloaded before that press.

**Which build.** Picked from what the GPU probe actually found, not from the platform:
CUDA where `nvidia-smi` answers and the card can run it, Vulkan for any other GPU, Metal
on Apple Silicon, CPU where there is no evidence of anything else. A slow engine that runs
beats a fast one that fails to start. llama.cpp's CUDA build is CUDA 13, which needs a
GTX 16 / RTX 20 series card or newer (compute capability 7.5) and driver 580 or newer, so
an older card or driver is recommended Vulkan and told why. The picker says CUDA is
roughly 15-20% faster than Vulkan on NVIDIA (a rough public figure, not yet measured on
our hardware); it is also the bigger download, about 550 MB on Windows with NVIDIA's CUDA
runtime against Vulkan's 30 MB. A supported NVIDIA machine on a Vulkan or CPU build is
offered **Switch to CUDA** on the Model server card. Every other build
for your machine stays in the list if you disagree. If you already have a `llama-server`,
point at it instead: Nekko Agent will run it and never update or remove it.

**No Visual Studio, ever.** The Windows builds of llama.cpp and stable-diffusion.cpp, and
Nekko's own engine daemon, need the Microsoft Visual C++ Runtime (`MSVCP140.dll`,
`VCRUNTIME140.dll`), not Visual Studio. The installer carries those DLLs beside the daemon
(about 1 MB), and on a PC without the Visual C++ Redistributable they are copied in beside
the engine before it starts. If an engine still dies for a missing DLL, the error says so
and links Microsoft's 25 MB redistributable.

**Where models come from.** A short curated list answers "what should I run"; search
covers everything else, straight against Hugging Face with no account. Each model expands
into its real builds with their real download sizes. Downloads resume after an
interruption and only land once the file parses as a GGUF, so a half-finished model never
shows up looking complete. A GGUF you already have is adopted without being copied, and
pointing the models folder at an existing library adopts everything in it.

**One address, several models.** The engine serves on `http://127.0.0.1:11500/v1` by
default, with a `llama-server` process per loaded model behind it. Several models stay
resident; a request for one that is not loaded loads it; an idle one is evicted on a
timer; and the address survives every load and unload. It is OpenAI-compatible, so point
Claude Code, Cursor, Continue or anything else at it and name a model from `/v1/models`.

**Two ways to configure a load.** *Simple* asks one question, how much of this machine
the model may use, and solves it into a real context length, GPU offload and KV cache
type, then says what it chose and what it costs. *Advanced* is every llama.cpp flag:
context, GPU layers, KV cache type, parallel slots, flash attention, batch and physical
batch, threads, mmap and mlock, RoPE base and scale, seed, idle TTL. They are the same
state, so moving one moves the other, and either can be saved as that model's default.

**Seeing what is loaded from anywhere.** The Agents view's **Panels** dock has a **Local
models** monitor, under Hardware: each model the engine holds in memory, whether it runs on
the GPU, split across GPU and CPU (with the layer count, in amber), or on the CPU, plus its
context and footprint. **Settings** on a row opens Nekko Server with that model's drawer
unfolded on *Advanced*, where **Runs on** (GPU only, Hybrid, CPU only) lives. The chat's
right panel has the same jump as **All settings** inside each model under Model settings.
Switch the monitor off in the dock's **Configure** menu. Changing a setting reloads the
model, which interrupts a reply it is generating.

**The Server tab** carries port, whether it is reachable from your network or only this
computer, an API key, allowed browser origins, how many models may be resident, the idle
timeout, load-on-demand, start-with-the-app, and the models folder. The defaults are
loopback-only with no key, which is safe; binding to the network is a deliberate act and
the app says what it means next to the setting. **A network bind requires a key**: the
engine refuses to listen on your network with the key empty, and picking **This computer
and my network** with no key set fills one in for you (a key you already typed is kept).
Send it as a Bearer token from the apps you point at the engine.

Because the engine holds the file, it reads the GGUF header directly, so the projection
below is **exact** for its own models where it has to report parts of itself as unknown
for somebody else's.

## Servers you already run

### What each one can do

They are not the same shape, and the app does not pretend they are.

| | Nekko engine | Ollama | LM Studio | vLLM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Start / stop from here | yes | yes | yes | **no**, connect only |
| Load a model on demand | yes | yes | yes | no, one model per process |
| Set context per load | yes | yes | yes | at launch only |
| Set GPU offload | yes | yes | yes | at launch only |
| Parallel slots | **per load** | restart required | no | at launch only |
| KV cache type | **per load** | restart required | no | at launch only |
| Reports per-model VRAM | **measured** | **yes** | no | no |
| Layer geometry for the planner | **from the file** | **yes** | no | no |
| Batch, threads, flash attention, rope | **yes** | no | no | at launch only |
| Installs the engine for you | **yes** | no | no | no |
| Downloads models for you | **yes** | yes | no | no |

Of the servers you bring yourself, **Ollama** is the most controllable and the only one
that reports its own CPU spill.
`/api/ps` gives both the model's total size and how much of it is in VRAM, and the gap
between those two numbers is exactly what did not fit. `/api/show` publishes the layer
count, KV head count, and embedding length, which is what lets the planner compute an
exact KV cache rather than an estimate.

**LM Studio** keeps most of its control surface in the `lms` CLI, so Nekko Agent drives
that: `lms server start` and `lms server stop` are a real lifecycle, and `lms load`
carries the context length and GPU share. It publishes no layer geometry anywhere, so
its projections are partial (see below). Driving it needs the CLI on the same machine as
the server, so a remote LM Studio can be read but not controlled.

**vLLM** is deliberately connect-existing only. It serves one model per process with
everything fixed by the launch command, and it is Linux plus NVIDIA plus Python in
practice. Nekko Agent detects it, shows its live `/metrics`, and can stop it, but never
starts it: instead the fit drawer renders the exact `vllm serve` command for you to run.
Nothing that could not be verified against real hardware ships as a working button.

### When a card lists no models

A card whose model list fails says why instead of "No models found." A server that does not
answer reads *"Ollama didn't answer at http://localhost:11434. Is it running?"*; any other
failure shows the provider's own message, such as a 401 from a refused key, unless the
connection test above it already says why. **Retry**
re-tests the connection and asks for the list again. A card with more than eight models
gets a filter box.

## Reading the fit bar

The bar stacks what the model needs against what the device has free:

- **Weights**, the model's actual size. Taken from what the server reports or the file on
  disk, never computed from a parameter count times a quantization width, which is wrong
  for mixed-precision builds like `Q4_K_M`.
- **KV cache**, the conversation's memory: `2 x layers x kvHeads x headDim x context x
  bytesPerElement x parallelSlots`.
- **Runtime overhead**, compute buffers and the server's own reserve.

The marker line is where the device's free memory runs out. Anything drawn past it has to
live in system RAM instead.

## The verdicts

| Verdict | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Fits** | Everything runs on the GPU with room to spare. |
| **Tight** | It fits, but a long conversation may start spilling. |
| **Spills to CPU** | Part of the model runs on the CPU. It works, several times slower. |
| **Will not load** | It does not fit even using system memory, or the context exceeds the model's own maximum. |
| **Unknown** | The server did not report enough to project it. |

**Unknown is a real answer, not a bug.** Nekko Agent will not infer a model's memory use
from its name. If the layer count is missing, it says so and names what is missing. A
confident wrong number costs you a long load and every number after it.

Where the weights are known but the geometry is not, which is the usual LM Studio case,
the answer is partial rather than absent: the real weights figure is shown, and if the
weights alone overflow the machine the will-not-load verdict is still certain.

The planner never blocks a load. A will-not-load verdict warns clearly and still lets you
proceed. The estimate can be wrong, and it is your machine.

## Why a model spills to the CPU

Three things push a model off the GPU, in roughly this order of surprise:

1. **Context length.** The KV cache grows linearly with context. Going from 8k to 64k
   multiplies it eightfold, and past a point the cache is larger than the model.
2. **Parallel slots.** Every concurrent slot gets its own full KV cache. Raising
   `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` from 1 to 4 quadruples the cache at the same context, which is
   why a model that fit yesterday can stop fitting today with nothing else changed.
3. **Something else already resident.** The planner measures against *free* memory, not
   total, so another loaded model counts against you.

The suggestion chips fix these in that order, and each one is re-planned before being
offered, so clicking a suggestion always improves the verdict.

## Apple Silicon

A Mac shares one memory pool between the CPU and GPU. The budget is therefore system
memory, and Nekko Agent never adds a "VRAM" figure on top of RAM, which would make a
64 GB Mac look like it has 128 GB. The fit drawer says so explicitly when it applies.

## Multiple GPUs

Two 12 GB cards are not one 24 GB card. Without tensor parallelism a model has to fit on
a single device, so the planner measures against the roomiest one and says that it is not
pooling them. Only vLLM can split a model across cards, through `--tensor-parallel-size`.

## Settings that need a restart

Some settings are read only when the server starts. Ollama's parallelism
(`OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL`) and KV cache type (`OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE`) are both like this.
The Advanced section shows them with the exact environment line to set and marks them
restart-required, rather than offering a control that would quietly not apply.

`OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0` roughly halves KV cache memory, which is often the cheapest
way to fit a longer context.

## Stopping a server

A server Nekko Agent started is stopped with its own handle, cleanly, and it will not
outlive the app. A server that was already running when Nekko Agent found it is somebody
else's process: stopping that one asks first and names what it would end, because the
thing holding port 11434 might be a service you depend on.

LM Studio is the exception that needs no such warning, since it has a real shutdown
command rather than a process to kill.

## Long tasks on a small context window

A local model is often loaded with an 8k or 32k context, and an agent fills that in a few
steps: one large file read or one noisy build log is most of it. Nekko Agent keeps the work
going rather than stopping when the window fills:

- **It uses the window the model was loaded with**, not the model's advertised maximum.
  LM Studio and the Nekko engine report it in their model list, and Ollama reports it for a
  loaded model. For anything that reports nothing, it falls back to a guess from the name.
- **Older tool output is left out of the request** once the conversation nears 80% of that
  window. The oldest large results (file reads, command output) are replaced, in what is sent,
  by a one-line note saying how much was there; the chat itself keeps everything, and the model
  can simply run the tool again if it needs that output back.
- **If the server still says the prompt is too long**, the request is sent once more with all
  of the older tool output left out.
- **If that is not enough, the chat compacts and carries on by itself.** The older part of the
  conversation is summarized, and the agent is asked to continue from the summary. This happens
  at most twice in a row before the chat waits for you, so a model that cannot make progress
  does not loop.

Giving the model more room is still the best fix. Raise its context when you load it (the
Models page shows what that costs in memory), and `OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0` roughly halves
the memory a longer context needs.

## Pictures and models that cannot see

Only a vision model with its projector file (`mmproj-*.gguf`) beside it can look at a
picture. The Nekko engine tells the app which of its models have one, so for a text-only
model such as Qwen3 4B the composer greys out **Photo / Video** and says why.

A picture can still end up in a text-only chat: you attached it while a vision model was
picked and then switched, or you used a server the app cannot classify. Such a server
rejects every request that carries an image, and the image stays in the conversation, so
before this guard the chat failed on every later message too. Now, when the model is known
not to take images, each picture is sent as a one-line note ("1 image attachment omitted:
this model does not accept image input") and the chat keeps working. The picture stays in
the chat itself, so switching back to a vision model sends it again.

A server that does not say what its models take still receives the pictures. If such a
model refuses them, click **Delete last message** in the failure notice (or **Delete** on
the message itself). That removes the message with the picture and anything after it, and
the chat answers again. You can then ask again without the picture, or switch to a model
with vision input.

## What is not here yet

Browsing and downloading models from inside the app, and a bundled inference engine so a
fresh install can run a model with nothing else present, are both planned as separate
pieces of work. Today Nekko Agent manages the runtimes you already have.

---

<!-- https://nekkoagent.com/docs/subscriptions -->

# Subscription sign-in

Nekko Agent can run chat turns on your existing Claude (Pro/Max) or ChatGPT (Plus/Pro/Business) subscription instead of a metered API key. The subscription path is optional: API keys remain available for Anthropic and OpenAI, and local model servers (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM) still cost $0.

## How it works

The host-side OAuth service runs the sign-in flow:

1. **Claude** - We use the same public OAuth client that Claude Code uses. After you click "Sign in with Claude", the app opens a browser to `https://claude.com/cai/oauth/authorize` and starts a loopback listener on a local port. After you authorize, Anthropic redirects to the listener with an authorization code. The host exchanges that code for an access token and stores it.

2. **ChatGPT / Codex** - We use the public OAuth client that the Codex CLI uses. The app opens `https://auth.openai.com/oauth/authorize` and tries to listen on `http://localhost:1455/auth/callback` (the registered redirect for that client). After authorization, OpenAI returns an access token, a refresh token, and an `id_token`. The host decodes the `id_token` to extract your ChatGPT account id, which the backend requires.

The host keeps the actual access and refresh tokens in `tokens.json` inside the data directory. At chat time, the host resolves a fresh access token and injects it into the request. The renderer only ever sees a sanitized status object: connected, account id, token key, and expiry. It never sees or stores the token itself.

## More than one account

You can sign in more than one plan from the same vendor, for example a personal Claude plan and a work one. Each gets its own provider, its own token and its own usage limits. To tell them apart, the app shows the email each one is signed in as next to its name, as in `Anthropic (Claude) · you@example.com`, in the model picker, the Utilization panel and the Capacity list.

The email comes from the sign-in itself (Claude's sign-in response, or the ChatGPT `id_token`), stays in `tokens.json` next to the token, and is not part of a settings export. A plan signed in before this was added shows no email until you sign it in again. API keys, OpenRouter and tokens pasted from `claude setup-token` carry no email, so they show just the provider name.

## Caveats

Both OAuth clients are the same first-party clients used by the vendors' own CLI tools. Anthropic and OpenAI consumer terms are written around their own apps, so using a subscription token with a third-party app like Nekko Agent is off-label. The flows may stop working at any time if the vendor rotates a client id, changes a scope, or blocks the client.

Because of this, the subscription paths are offered as-is alongside the API key options, which are unaffected. The features are live-validated on the current versions of the vendor flows. If a flow breaks, the fallback paths below still work.

## Fallbacks

If the browser loopback fails, for example because another process is already using the port, the app falls back to the manual paste path:

- **Claude** - Copy the `code#state` string the authorization page shows and paste it into the manual code input.
- **ChatGPT** - If port 1455 is busy, the app switches to manual mode and you copy the code from the page.

You can also import a sign-in you already did with an official CLI:

- **Claude** - `claude setup-token` mints a long-lived token. Paste that token as the manual code.
- **Codex CLI** - `codex login` writes `~/.codex/auth.json`. The app can read it and import the same token shape.

If a subscription session expires, the provider card shows the expiry and a "Re-authenticate" button to sign in again.

## Security

- Tokens are stored in `tokens.json` under the Nekko Agent data directory. The file is created with mode `0600` and the host re-applies that permission on startup.
- `tokens.json` is never included in a settings export. The export contains only provider configuration (base URL, label, and the opaque `tokenKey`), not the access or refresh tokens.
- The host never sends token values to the renderer. The renderer can only request status, sign out, or re-auth through the host.
- Removing a subscription provider also deletes its stored token from the host.

---

<!-- https://nekkoagent.com/docs/usage-limits -->

# Usage limits and price estimates

This page explains where Nekko Agent's usage numbers come from and what they mean.

## Where the limit numbers come from

The app does not guess your usage. It asks the provider:

- **Claude (Anthropic subscription)** - Every subscription-mode response carries `anthropic-ratelimit-unified-*` headers that report the 5-hour, 7-day, and per-model 7-day windows. The host also polls `GET https://api.anthropic.com/api/oauth/usage` for the first paint and manual refreshes.

- **ChatGPT (Codex subscription)** - The host polls `GET https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/wham/usage` with the current Bearer token and `ChatGPT-Account-Id`. The endpoint returns optional `primary_window` and `secondary_window` usage, plus plan type and credits. These are slots, not fixed periods: a primary window can be weekly, and either slot can be absent or null. Each window's `limit_window_seconds` determines its identity and label. Reported durations of 18,000 and 604,800 seconds become `5-hour` and `7-day`, respectively, regardless of slot; other positive integer durations get explicit duration labels. Missing or invalid durations retain the usage/reset data under neutral `Primary usage` or `Secondary usage` labels; neither the slot nor time until reset is used to guess a period.

  Source: OpenAI's public Codex source at commit `b741e480e203f037ca726bc2a76d99a8e8668e66`: [nullable window slots](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/b741e480e203f037ca726bc2a76d99a8e8668e66/codex-rs/codex-backend-openapi-models/src/models/rate_limit_status_details.rs#L21-L34), [window duration field](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/b741e480e203f037ca726bc2a76d99a8e8668e66/codex-rs/codex-backend-openapi-models/src/models/rate_limit_window_snapshot.rs#L14-L22), [duration conversion](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/b741e480e203f037ca726bc2a76d99a8e8668e66/codex-rs/backend-client/src/client.rs#L741-L753), and [duration-driven labels with neutral fallbacks](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/b741e480e203f037ca726bc2a76d99a8e8668e66/codex-rs/tui/src/chatwidget/rate_limits.rs#L103-L145). Nekko uses exact reported durations rather than Codex's approximate label matching.

Both providers are normalized into the same `SubscriptionLimits` shape in `packages/shared/src/limits.ts`. That shape has no unknown/general-duration scope: ChatGPT durations of at least seven days use `weekly`, shorter durations use `session`, and unknown durations use `session` only as a compatibility fallback. The displayed label, not that fallback scope, describes the reported period.

## Live reads, not estimates

The numbers in the chat header chip and the Models card are live reads from the provider. They update after each subscription response and on a throttled poll. Nekko Agent does not extrapolate or predict your usage locally; if a provider does not return a window, that window is simply not shown.

## Utilization and Budget on the Agents wall

Utilization deduplicates enabled Claude subscription entries with the same nonempty token key, preferring the Anthropic provider entry. This only changes the displayed account list, not saved providers, credentials or routing. Different accounts/token keys and API-key entries stay separate.

Budget defaults to **1m**. Its ranges use inclusive **UTC** days: today, 1wk (7 days), 1m (30), 6m (180), 1y (365), and all-time through today. The active button has an accent tint and pressed state. All recorded details follow that selection: estimated API spend, input/output tokens, top agent by API cost, local tokens, local/subscription savings, fallback and unpriced-token counts, and which used models appear in the pricing comparison. Catalog unit prices and the selected fallback are reference/configuration values, not range totals. Older hosts without daily detail show unavailable details rather than substituting lifetime totals.

Savings are estimated API equivalents before subscription fees, hardware and electricity, not actual net savings. Local and subscription usage has $0 incremental recorded API spend. Unknown local models use the explicitly chosen fallback or remain unpriced; unpriced tokens are excluded from savings.

The 2026-10-13 batch is implemented, unit and fixture interaction tested with TS/Rust daily-summary golden parity coverage. Image and motion inspection are pending; parent-owned landing is still outstanding.

## Off-label caveat

The Anthropic and ChatGPT usage endpoints used here are documented by or reverse-engineered from the providers' subscription flows. They can change, move, or stop returning data at any time. Nekko Agent is not affiliated with Anthropic or OpenAI, and the readouts are provided as a convenience for subscribers, not as an official feature of those services.

## Prices are list estimates, not a bill

`MODEL_PRICING` in `packages/shared/src/limits.ts` is a table of published list prices, matched by model id substring. The per-model labels (`$X/$Y per MTok`) and the session total in the chat header are estimates only.

Your actual provider bill may differ because of taxes, discounts, cached-token pricing, batch pricing, enterprise agreements, image or tool-token costs, or mid-rate changes. Local models (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM) and subscription providers are shown as `Free` or `Included in plan` because they are not metered through an API key in Nekko Agent.

## Limits are provider-side

Nekko Agent can only read and surface the limits that Anthropic and OpenAI return. It cannot raise, reset, or bypass them. If a window is reported as rate limited, that state comes from the provider; Nekko Agent does not create or remove the limit.

---

<!-- https://nekkoagent.com/docs/remote -->

# Phone remote control

Drive the Nekko Agent running on your computer from your phone: start and manage chats, watch and steer
training runs and goals, approve risky commands, and get a push when a long run finishes. Inference
and tools always execute on **your** machine, under its guardrails; the phone is a thin client.

## How it works

```
[ Phone ]  --TLS-->  [ relay ]  <--outbound WSS--  [ your computer (agent) ]
```

- Your computer **dials out** to a relay and claims a room. No inbound ports, no port-forwarding.
- Your phone connects to the same relay with the pairing credentials.
- Every payload is **end-to-end encrypted** (AES-GCM, key derived from the pairing secret). The
  relay routes ciphertext; it cannot read prompts, replies, files, or model output.
- On top of the encrypted transport, every device must pass a **handshake against your computer's
  device registry**: new devices enroll only through a **single-use pairing code that expires in
  10 minutes**, and your computer answers each device individually (never broadcast).

## Pairing a phone

1. On your computer: **Settings → Remote access → Enable** (the managed relay is prefilled; or
   paste your self-hosted relay URL), then **Pair a device**.
2. On your phone: scan the QR in the Nekko Agent app (**Computers → Pair a computer**), or with the
   phone's camera app, which hands the `nekko-agent-pair:` link to the Nekko Agent app. Without the
   app, the pairing link also opens the web app in a browser over the relay, but it is limited to
   what a phone may do (below), so most desktop screens there are unavailable.
3. The phone shows up under **Paired devices**, with a live connection dot.

## The phone app

> **Native apps.** The phone apps are moving to platform-native code: Kotlin / Jetpack Compose in
> `apps/android` (pairing, chats, live replies, approvals and questions; no phone models yet) and
> SwiftUI in `apps/ios`. The Expo app described below stays as the reference until they reach parity.
>
> The Android app looks like your desktop by default: **Settings → Appearance → Same as computer**
> uses the computer's light or dark theme and its accent color, and follows a change on the
> computer right away. Pick **Phone setting**, **Light** or **Dark** to choose on the phone instead;
> that choice is kept on the phone. Only the theme, theme preset and the two accent colors are sent
> for this (the `appearance:updated` event), never the rest of the computer's settings.
>
> The Android app's **Settings** also has a **Computers** row, which opens the list of paired
> computers (rename, switch, forget, pair another), and an **About** section with the installed
> version and the open-source licenses of the app and the libraries it ships.
>
> **New chat defaults** (Android): **Settings → New chats** picks the computer the app connects to
> when it starts (default: the one used last) and, for each computer, the model New chat opens with
> (default: the computer's own default model). They are saved on the phone; the computer's settings
> don't change. If that model is no longer offered, New chat says so and uses the computer's default.
> **Share to Nekko** (Android): in any app's share menu, pick **Nekko Agent** to start a new chat
> with the shared text or link. You can edit it on the New chat screen; after you start the chat it
> waits in the message box and you send it yourself. Nekko never sends shared text on its own, and
> it is kept only in memory until then. Text and links only for now, up to 20,000 characters.
> **Vibration** (Android): while the app is open, the phone vibrates when the agent needs your
> approval (two pulses) or asks you a question (one long pulse). In **Settings → Vibration** you can
> also turn on a short tap when a reply finishes and three taps when it fails, or switch any of them
> off. It never vibrates in silent mode or Do Not Disturb, or while the app is in the background.
>
> **Your computer's settings from the phone** (Android): **Settings → On <computer>** changes three
> of the computer's own settings: the chat mode for new chats (Ask, Guardrails or YOLO; YOLO asks once
> before switching), what a long-press on a chat does (Complete, which moves it to Completed, or
> Delete), and whether deleting asks first. They are saved on the computer, the same settings as in
> its Settings. A long-press on a chat in the list then completes or deletes it on the computer.
>
> **All your chats, grouped like the desktop** (Android): the chat list shows every chat on the
> computer, completed ones included, in the same groups as the desktop's agent sidebar: **General**
> first, then one group per project folder. Tap a group's name to fold it. Each group lists its
> active chats, then **Show completed (N)**, which opens the chats completed there (struck through,
> newest first). Tap a completed chat to read it; its message box is replaced by **Restore**, and a
> long-press on it offers Restore or Delete. Completing or restoring a chat on the computer shows up
> on the phone the next time the list refreshes: when a reply finishes, when you pull down, or when
> you come back to the app.
>
> **Photos and dictation** (Android): the **+** on the left of a chat's message box opens **Dictate**,
> **Image from files** (the phone's photo picker; Nekko only sees the photos you pick) and **Take
> photo** (the phone's camera app). Up to 4 photos go with the next message, shown as thumbnails you
> can remove; they are scaled to 1600 px and sent end-to-end encrypted to the computer, which hands
> them to the chat's model like a photo pasted on the desktop. A text-only model doesn't see them.
