> The photos stay in the message's bubble on the phone too, as small previews the computer makes
> (the newest 40 photos in a chat, including ones attached on the computer); an older photo shows as
> a plain tile, and the full-size original stays on the computer.
>
> **Dictation** (Android): tap **+ → Dictate**, speak, and tap ■ (or stop
> at 30 seconds). The words go into the message box for you to check and send; nothing is sent by
> itself. By default the speech is turned into text by **Nekko Voice on your computer** (Whisper,
> end-to-end encrypted, the audio never reaches anyone else); install and switch it on there under
> **Settings → Nekko Voice**. When the computer can't, the phone's own speech recognizer is used,
> which on many phones sends the audio to Google. **Settings → Dictation** on the phone lets you use
> only the computer, only the phone, or turn the microphone off.
>
> **Skills** (Android): type `/` at the start of a chat's message box to see the skills on your
> computer: the built-in ones, those you installed from the Marketplace for Nekko Agent, and the
> ones Nekko Agent found in your Claude Code, Codex or Gemini skill folders. Pick one, add details
> if you like, and send. Nothing is copied to the phone: the list is read from the computer each
> time you open a chat, so a skill you install or remove there shows up on the phone right away,
> and the computer adds the skill's instructions itself, so they never leave it. `/goal` is not
> offered on the phone, and skills are installed and removed on the computer.
>
> **Long chats on the phone**: the phone gets the newest 300 messages of a chat, without the
> screenshots inside tool results and with long tool output shortened to 4,000 characters, so even
> a very long agent run opens in seconds. The chat says how many earlier messages, characters and
> images stayed on the computer; open it there for the full detail.
>
> The Android app is **locked by default**: every time you open it, or come back to it, it asks for
> your fingerprint, face or the phone's screen lock (PIN, pattern or password) before it shows
> anything. While it is locked nothing can be read or approved, and the recent-apps preview shows a
> plain cover instead of your chats. After a restart it doesn't connect to your computer until you unlock. Turn it off in
> **Settings → Security → App lock**; turning it off asks for the same check first. Screenshots and screen
> recording of the app work as usual, lock on or off; on Android 14 and later the screenshot toolbar
> some phones show afterwards (Samsung) no longer hides the app behind the cover. A phone with no screen lock can't be locked;
> Settings says so and links to the phone's security settings.
>
> The Android app **reconnects by itself** as soon as the phone changes network (Wi-Fi to mobile data,
> airplane mode off), instead of waiting out its retry delay. While a chat on your computer is running,
> **Settings → Connection → Stay connected while a chat runs** (on by default) keeps the app connected
> after you leave it, with a silent "Staying connected · 1 chat running on Mac" notification that goes
> away as soon as the reply is done. **Notify me** (on by default; Android 13+ asks for permission)
> sends a notification when a reply finishes or fails, or a chat waits for your approval or answer,
> while you're out of the app. Notifications say what happened and in which chat, never the reply, the
> command or the question; with the app lock on they don't name the chat either, and tapping one opens
> the chat through the lock. Without push (not built yet), these only arrive while the phone is still
> connected. If Android restricts Nekko in the background, Settings says so and opens the app's
> system page.

The iOS and Android app (`apps/mobile`) is built for the phone rather than being the desktop on a
small screen: your computer's chats with **Working** / **Needs you** badges, new chats on any of the
computer's models and folders, live replies, **Allow this?** cards for risky commands, the agent's
questions as tap-to-answer choices, follow-ups that queue while a run is going, and Stop. It can
pair several computers and talks to one at a time.

It also runs **models on the phone itself** (llama.cpp, curated small GGUF models from Hugging Face
sized to the phone's memory), so you can keep chatting when the computer is off. Those chats never
leave the phone and don't use the relay.

**The native iPhone app** (`apps/ios`, SwiftUI) does the same over the same encrypted relay, and
adds what only iOS can: a **Live Activity** for each running chat on the Lock Screen and in the
Dynamic Island, with **Allow / Deny** for a waiting tool and **Stop**; notifications with Allow /
Deny actions while the app is in the background (Allow asks you to unlock first); photo attachments;
and dictation (Whisper on your computer when Nekko Voice is installed, else the iPhone's own
speech recognition). Its pairing screen leads with Tailscale and shows whether Tailscale is on on
the iPhone. If a Tailscale relay can't be reached, the app says which side is the problem:
Tailscale is off on the phone, or the computer isn't answering. With the app lock on (Face ID or
passcode, on by default), the Lock Screen and notifications never show chat titles or commands.

On the phone, the pairing key and the derived encryption key live in the iOS Keychain / Android
Keystore. The app drops any provider API keys your computer sends with its settings and never
stores them.

Manage devices from the same card: **rename** them, **revoke** one instantly (it's kicked live and
denied from then on), or **Rotate secret** to cryptographically reset the room, which unpairs
everything at once. A revoked phone can come back only the way a new one does: choose **Pair a
device** on the computer and scan the new QR from the phone (the one-time code is the proof). Older
computers refused a revoked phone even then; on those, **Rotate secret** first.

Remote access survives restarts: if it was enabled, the agent reconnects when Nekko Agent starts.

## What a paired phone can do

Your computer decides what a paired phone may ask for, whatever the phone app does: locking the
phone app is not the boundary, your computer is. A phone can use your chats and nothing that
changes how the computer itself is set up:

- **Allowed:** list, open, start, complete and delete chats; send, queue and stop messages; answer
  approvals and the agent's questions; pick a model from the computer's providers and a folder from
  its list; voice status and transcription; and a few settings (below).
- **Never allowed from a phone:** wiping data or resetting settings, remote access itself (pairing,
  revoking, rotating the secret), terminals, reading or writing files, accepting or reverting changes, adding or removing folders, installing
  or removing voice models, connecting or disconnecting connectors, provider keys and sign-ins, MCP
  servers and hooks. Everything not on the allowed list is refused too, with an error that starts
  *Not allowed from a paired phone*.
- **Settings a phone may change:** the chat mode for new chats (Ask, Guardrails or YOLO), what the chat pane's top-right button does (Complete or Delete),
  whether deleting asks first, and voice on/off and its language. An update that touches any other
  setting is refused as a whole: nothing in it is applied.
- **Settings a phone can read:** only the theme and accents, the default and starred models, and
  the settings above. API keys, tokens, provider details, folders, hooks, guardrails and your
  instructions never leave the computer this way; provider lists arrive as name and type only.
- **A chat's changes, read only, only if you allow it:** with *Let phones see changes* on (off
  unless you turn it on, in Remote access on the computer), a phone can see a diff of the files the
  agent changed in a chat. Your computer works out the diff and sends only that: short paths, a
  capped number of lines, and files that may hold secrets (`.env`, keys, `.ssh`, `.aws`) counted but
  never shown. A phone still can't accept or revert changes or read any other file.
- **One chat's options:** a phone can change a chat's model, title, pin and tags, complete it, and
  switch it between Ask, Guardrails and YOLO, but not its tools, isolation or
  offline/incognito switches. Messages cannot attach files from the computer.

## Security model, honestly stated

| Threat | Defense |
|---|---|
| Relay operator reads your traffic | Impossible by construction: E2E encryption, relay sees ciphertext only |
| Stranger connects to your room | Needs the pairing secret (128-bit) for transport auth, then a registered device or a live pairing code |
| Leaked/stale pairing link | The one-time code is single-use and expires in 10 min; the link is scrubbed from the phone's URL/history after pairing |
| Lost/stolen phone | The Android app asks for the phone's fingerprint, face or screen lock every time it opens. Revoke the phone in Settings: kicked immediately, denied afterward, push token dropped |
| Revoked device replays old creds | The agent refuses its handshake and unicasts nothing to it; it gets back in only with a fresh one-time pairing code from the computer's owner; rotate the secret for a full cryptographic reset |
| Malicious relay withholding/reordering | Availability only; it still can't read or forge frames (AES-GCM auth) |
| Phone asks for something dangerous | Your computer only serves the phone allowlist above (no wipe, settings reset, remote-access changes, terminals, file writes); tool calls run on your machine under your guardrails/sandbox and chat mode |

What the relay does see: connection metadata (IPs, timing, frame sizes), the room code, and, if you
enable push, device push tokens plus the content-free fact "a run finished". That's the whole list,
and it's why relayed local-model use is inherently zero-data-retention for content.

## Choosing a relay

How the Android and iOS apps each handle the connection (URL rules, pairing, reconnects, push, background) is compared in [phone-connection.md](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/blob/main/docs/phone-connection.md).

### Managed relay (default): `wss://nekko-agent-relay.fly.dev`

Zero setup; free during beta with per-connection rate limits. When Nekko Agent Cloud launches, the
managed relay becomes part of the paid plans (it already supports gating via
`NEKKO_RELAY_AUTHZ_URL`), while self-hosting stays free forever.

### Private relay over Tailscale (free, no account, nothing hosted)

If your phone and computer are both on a [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com) network, you do not
need a hosted relay at all: run the relay **on the computer** and bind it to the computer's
Tailscale address. Only devices on your tailnet can reach it, Tailscale encrypts the hop
(WireGuard), and the app's end-to-end layer still sits on top. This is how free remote-desktop
tools such as Moonlight stay free: nothing runs in the cloud, the two ends find each other over a
network you already own.

**In the desktop app:** Settings → Remote access → **Relay on this computer** → **Start relay**.
The app finds this computer's Tailscale address (any interface in `100.64.0.0/10`), starts the
bundled relay bound to that address only, and shows the URL phones use. That is the MagicDNS name
(for example `ws://gomi.tailfd6474.ts.net:4400`) when the Tailscale CLI reports one, else the
`100.x.y.z` address. **Use this relay** fills it in; then Enable, **Pair a device**, and scan the QR
from the phone with Tailscale switched on.

- **It stays on:** once started it comes back with the app.
- **It waits for Tailscale:** with Tailscale off it binds nowhere and waits, and starts when
  Tailscale connects.
- **It follows address changes:** it moves when the tailnet address changes.
- **It says why it isn't running:** for example Tailscale off, or the port (4400) already in use.

It runs as its own process (`out/main/relay.js`, under the app's own runtime) and exits with the
app. It has no push keys, so phones get no "finished" notifications through it; the in-app
connection and Live Activities while the app is open work as usual.

**Headless or without the desktop app**, the scripts do the same by hand:

```bash
npm run relay:tailscale        # Windows (PowerShell); or scripts/private-relay.sh on macOS/Linux
```

The script prints the URL to paste into **Settings → Remote access**. Either way the relay only
listens on the Tailscale interface, so agent enrollment without an access token
(`NEKKO_RELAY_ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED=1` in the script) is safe here; never use that flag on a public
bind.

The computer refuses a plain `ws://` relay on the open internet, whether you press Enable or start
a headless agent with `NEKKO_RELAY_URL`. It uses the same rule as the phones, below.

Plain `ws://` is fine on a tailnet: the transport is already encrypted end to end by WireGuard, and
the app's own end-to-end encryption sits on top. The Expo iOS app ships with Expo's default App
Transport Security (arbitrary loads allowed). **The native iPhone app allows plain `ws://` only toward
private networks**: Tailscale (`*.ts.net` names and `100.x.y.z` addresses) and your local network.
It refuses a `ws://` link to anything on the open internet before dialing; use `wss://` there. **The Android app allows plain `ws://` only to Tailscale
MagicDNS names (`*.ts.net`)**, so use the name the script prints (`ws://gomi.tailfd6474.ts.net:4400`),
not the `100.x.y.z` address: Android can't allow an IP range, and blocks the bare address. If you
use an address the phone can't reach (a bare Tailscale IP, `localhost`, or any other plain `ws://`
host), the Android app says so on its pairing screen and in the chat list instead of spinning on
"Connecting…". If you prefer `wss://`, enable **HTTPS certificates** in the tailnet's DNS settings
and either put `tailscale serve --bg 4400` in front (needs Serve enabled once per tailnet) or
terminate TLS with `tailscale cert` on your own proxy.

Trade-offs: the computer must be awake and Tailscale running; push notifications need APNs/FCM
keys on this relay like any other; Tailscale's free plan covers up to 100 devices and 3 users.

### Self-host (free forever, one command)

The relay is a tiny stateless Node service; anything that runs a container can host it.

**Docker**

```bash
docker run -d --name nekko-agent-relay -p 4400:4400 --restart unless-stopped \
  -e NEKKO_RELAY_ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED=1 \
  ghcr.io/nekko-labs/nekko-agent-relay:latest
```

**Docker Compose**

```yaml
services:
  nekko-agent-relay:
    image: ghcr.io/nekko-labs/nekko-agent-relay:latest
    ports: ["4400:4400"]
    environment:
      NEKKO_RELAY_ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED: "1"
    restart: unless-stopped
```

**Coolify** (recommended if you already run one): add a new service → Docker image
`ghcr.io/nekko-labs/nekko-agent-relay:latest`, expose port 4400, attach a domain, and let Coolify's
proxy terminate TLS. Point Nekko Agent at `wss://relay.your-domain.com`.

**Fly.io**: `fly deploy -c apps/relay/fly.toml` from a repo checkout. Keep it at **one machine**
(`fly scale count 1`): rooms live in a machine's memory, so agent and phone must land on the same
instance.

Put any self-hosted relay behind TLS (`wss://`) for internet use; the E2E layer protects content
regardless, but TLS also protects the transport-auth query string. Then paste the URL into
**Settings → Remote access** before enabling.

Environment knobs:

| Env | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `NEKKO_RELAY_PORT` / `NEKKO_RELAY_HOST` | Bind (default `0.0.0.0:4400`) |
| `APNS_KEY_P8` / `APNS_KEY_ID` / `APNS_TEAM_ID` | Enable iOS push |
| `FCM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT` | Enable Android push (service-account JSON) |
| `NEKKO_RELAY_AUTHZ_URL` | Gate agent enrollment on a Nekko Agent Cloud account (managed hosting) |
| `NEKKO_RELAY_ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED=1` | Explicitly allow unauthenticated agent enrollment for trusted/private deployments; otherwise agent enrollment is disabled when no authz URL is configured |

The relay validates device IDs as UUIDs and push tokens as non-empty platform
tokens. A connected device cannot replace another connection's push token for
the same device ID. Keep the relay behind TLS (`wss://`) and do not enable the
unauthenticated mode on a public endpoint.

## Headless agents

A machine without a screen (server, homelab box) can expose itself with the relay-agent mode:

```bash
NEKKO_RELAY_URL=wss://your-relay NEKKO_ROOM=myroom NEKKO_PAIR_KEY=<secret> npx nekko-agent
```

It prints a one-time pairing code (10 minutes) at boot and keeps the same persistent device
registry as the desktop app.

---

<!-- https://nekkoagent.com/docs/cli -->

# Nekko Agent CLI and MCP

The CLI makes the Nekko Agent host a subagent for Devin, Claude Code, Codex,
Cursor, and other harnesses. It uses the same host engine as the desktop and
web editions.

## Install and target

Published package:

```bash
npm install --global nekko-agent   # publishing with the next release
npx nekko-agent status
```

From a checkout:

```bash
npm install
npm run build --workspace=apps/cli
node apps/cli/dist/index.js status
```

Use `nekko-agent` after a global install or linking the built package, or invoke
the bundled binary from `apps/cli/dist/index.js`. Without `--url`, the CLI runs
an in-process host
against `~/.nekko` (override with `NEKKO_DATA_DIR`). To drive a web edition,
use:

```bash
nekko-agent --url http://127.0.0.1:1440 --token "$NEKKO_TOKEN" status --json
```

`--url` can also be supplied as `NEKKO_URL`; `--token` can be supplied as
`NEKKO_TOKEN`.

## Safety and approval

Chat defaults to `--approve guardrails` (or `NEKKO_APPROVE=guardrails`).
Guardrails mode sets the session to `guardrails`: ordinary tools run, ask-rule
approvals are refused and reported as structured `blocked` entries, and the
turn continues. The result tells the harness to use `--approve yolo` when an
override is intentional.

`--approve yolo` explicitly opts into the previous unattended behavior. Deny
rules remain a hard floor in every mode. `--approve ask` prompts on the TTY;
it is an error when stdin is not a TTY.

These policies govern the agent tool loop, not every process the host can
launch. In particular, `bash` is not confined by `workspace-jail`; use the
host's deployment and workspace controls when granting an external harness
access.

## Commands

```text
status [--json]
sessions [--json]
chat "<prompt>" [--session ID] [--new] [--workspace ID] [--provider ID] [--model ID]
  [--approve guardrails|yolo|ask] [--json|--stream ndjson] [--timeout SECONDS] [--quiet]
workspace list|add PATH|remove ID|index ID|search ID QUERY [--json]
prompts [--json]
tasks list|add|run ID|delete ID [--json]
skills [--json]
skills install ID [--target nekko-agent|claude|codex] [--json]
tools [--json]
models [PROVIDER_ID] [--json]
local status|list [--json]
local search [QUERY] [--json]
local download OWNER/REPO [--quant LABEL] [--json]
local downloads [--active] | local cancel JOB_ID [--json]
local load MODEL_ID [--provider ID] [--ctx N] [--gpu-layers N] [--ttl SECONDS] [--json]
local unload MODEL_ID [--provider ID] | local start [--provider ID] | local stop [--provider ID] [--force]
train start NAME GOAL [--provider ID] [--model ID] [--workspace ID] [--json]
train status|hint ID TEXT|stop ID [--json]
watch [--session ID] [--json]
mcp
```

Prompts may be positional, piped through stdin (`nekko-agent chat -`), or loaded
from a file (`nekko-agent chat --file prompt.md`). `--quiet` suppresses human
progress on stderr.

## Machine output

`--json` emits exactly one JSON object on stdout. Chat objects have this shape:

```json
{
  "sessionId": "…",
  "provider": "…",
  "model": "…",
  "text": "…",
  "toolCalls": [{ "name": "read_file", "input": { "path": "README.md" } }],
  "blocked": [{ "ruleLabels": ["…"], "command": "…", "severity": "high", "reason": "…" }],
  "durationMs": 1234,
  "usage": { "inputTokens": 100, "outputTokens": 40 }
}
```

`--stream ndjson` emits one typed event per line:

```json
{"type":"text","delta":"Hello"}
{"type":"tool_call","call":{"name":"read_file","input":{"path":"README.md"}}}
{"type":"tool_result","toolCallId":"…","ok":true,"output":"…"}
{"type":"blocked","ruleLabels":["ask"],"command":"…","severity":"high","reason":"…"}
{"type":"done"}
```

Progress and diagnostics go to stderr. Other commands accept `--json`;
`watch --json` emits the same typed event objects as NDJSON and exits cleanly
when it receives Ctrl-C. Watch events are `text`, `tool_call`, `tool_result`,
`blocked`, `done`, and `error`; reasoning and usage-only events are omitted.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
| ---: | --- |
| 0 | Success |
| 2 | Usage or invalid flags |
| 3 | Nothing configured (provider/model missing) |
| 4 | Guardrail-blocked tool call |
| 5 | Provider/model failure |
| 6 | Chat timeout |
| 7 | Cannot reach or unauthorized against `--url` |

## MCP

Start the JSON-RPC stdio server:

```bash
node apps/cli/dist/index.js mcp
```

Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add nekko-agent -- node /abs/path/nekko-agent/apps/cli/dist/index.js mcp
```

Codex:

```bash
codex mcp add nekko-agent -- node /abs/path/nekko-agent/apps/cli/dist/index.js mcp
```

Cursor and generic `mcpServers` configuration:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "nekko-agent": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["/abs/path/nekko-agent/apps/cli/dist/index.js", "mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

`nekko-agent_chat` accepts the same `approve` policy as the CLI and defaults to
`guardrails`. `nekko-agent_train_start` also accepts an explicit `approve` argument;
unattended training that intentionally permits ask-rules must pass
`"approve": "yolo"`. The server negotiates MCP protocol versions, echoing a
supported client version and otherwise selecting its newest supported version.
`nekko-agent_task_create` exposes `title`, `prompt`, `kind`, `runAt`, `intervalMs`,
`workspaceId`, `providerId`, `modelId`, `condition`, and `keepAlive` directly;
`title`, `prompt`, and `kind` are required. A `nekko-agent_chat` result presents
the assistant reply first, followed by a metadata block containing session,
tool-call, blocked-entry, duration, and usage details.

The MCP tool list mirrors the CLI coverage: `nekko-agent_chat`,
`nekko-agent_list_sessions`, `nekko-agent_new_session`, `nekko-agent_get_session`,
`nekko-agent_workspace_list`, `nekko-agent_workspace_add`, `nekko-agent_workspace_remove`,
`nekko-agent_workspace_index`, `nekko-agent_workspace_search`,
`nekko-agent_prompts_list`, `nekko-agent_tasks_list`, `nekko-agent_task_create`,
`nekko-agent_task_run`, `nekko-agent_task_delete`, `nekko-agent_skills_list`,
`nekko-agent_skill_install`, `nekko-agent_tools_list`, `nekko-agent_models_list`,
`nekko-agent_train_start`, `nekko-agent_train_status`, `nekko-agent_train_hint`,
`nekko-agent_train_stop`, `nekko-agent_status`, and the local-model tools below.

### Local models

An MCP client can run a model on this machine without opening the app: check
what is installed and loaded, download a model, load it, send it work through
`nekko-agent_chat`, and unload it again. The CLI's `local` command does the same
from a terminal.

| Tool | CLI | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `nekko-agent_local_status` | `local status` | The built-in engine (installed, running, loaded models, memory budget) and every enabled local runtime (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM). |
| `nekko-agent_local_models` | `local list` | Models in the engine library: id, size, quantization, loaded, and whether it fits on the GPU (`full`, `partial`, `cpu`, `wont`). |
| `nekko-agent_model_search` | `local search` | Hugging Face GGUF repos the engine can download (the curated list with no query). |
| `nekko-agent_model_download` | `local download` | Start downloading one quantization; `Q4_K_M` (or the closest) when none is named. Returns a job id at once. |
| `nekko-agent_downloads` | `local downloads` | Progress of each download: state, percent, size, ETA. |
| `nekko-agent_download_cancel` | `local cancel` | Cancel a download. |
| `nekko-agent_model_load` | `local load` | Load a model; the engine starts itself if it is not running. Returns the `provider` and `model` to pass to `nekko-agent_chat`. |
| `nekko-agent_model_unload` | `local unload` | Unload a model to free memory. |
| `nekko-agent_runtime_start` | `local start` | Start the engine, or a runtime named by `providerId`. |
| `nekko-agent_runtime_stop` | `local stop` | Stop it. A server Nekko Agent did not start is refused with `needsConfirmation`; ask before retrying with `force`. |

Every tool targets the built-in engine unless it is given a `providerId` (CLI
`--provider`) for another local runtime; cloud providers are refused. Download,
load and stop are the same operations as the Model Server page and follow its
rules: a download is several GB more often than not, so compare its size with
the memory budget in `local_status` first.

Who keeps the model running depends on whether the app is open. With the app
serving, the engine is the app's and a loaded model stays loaded after the CLI
or MCP client exits. Without the app, `nekko-agent mcp` runs the engine itself
for the length of its session and stops it when the client disconnects, so no
model server is left behind. The one-shot `local load` and `local start`
commands need the app for that reason, and an in-process `local download` waits
until the files have landed.

A typical hand-off from Claude Code: "run qwen3 4B locally and have it review
this file" becomes `nekko-agent_local_models` (or `model_search` and
`model_download`, polling `nekko-agent_downloads`), then `nekko-agent_model_load`,
then `nekko-agent_chat` with the returned `provider` and `model`. A chat turn
carries the agent's system prompt and tool list, several thousand tokens, so a
model loaded with a very small `contextTokens` cannot answer one; leave it unset
for the engine default.

## Recipes

### Drive a repeated workflow

```bash
nekko-agent tasks add --title "daily review" --kind recurring \
  --interval-ms 86400000 --prompt "Review the current workspace diff and summarize risks" \
  --workspace "$WORKSPACE_ID" --provider "$PROVIDER" --model "$MODEL" --json
nekko-agent tasks list --json
nekko-agent tasks run TASK_ID --json
```

### Fan out several sessions

```bash
nekko-agent chat "Review security" --new --workspace "$W" --json > security.json &
nekko-agent chat "Review tests" --new --workspace "$W" --json > tests.json &
nekko-agent chat "Review API design" --new --workspace "$W" --json > api.json &
wait
```

### Hand off training and poll it

```bash
nekko-agent train start "ranking-v1" "Improve ranking accuracy" \
  --workspace "$W" --provider "$PROVIDER" --model "$MODEL" --json
nekko-agent train status --json
nekko-agent train hint RUN_ID "Try a larger validation split" --json
nekko-agent train stop RUN_ID --json
```

### Run a local model from a script

```bash
nekko-agent local status --json
nekko-agent local download unsloth/Qwen3-4B-GGUF --quant Q4_K_M --json
nekko-agent local downloads --active --json   # poll until done
nekko-agent local list --json                  # find the model id
nekko-agent local load "$MODEL_ID" --json
nekko-agent chat "Summarize README.md" --provider nekko-engine --model "$MODEL_ID" --new --json
nekko-agent local unload "$MODEL_ID" --json
```

---

<!-- https://nekkoagent.com/docs/automations -->

# Automations

An automation is a workflow that runs on its own: on a schedule, when something happens in a
connected app, or when you start it. They live in the **Workflows** tab. This page covers the
ready-made ones, how you hear about their runs, and how to stop them all at once. For building
your own step by step, see the Workflows tab's **How workflows work** strip; for running a repo's
CI on your machine, see [Local CI runner](https://nekkoagent.com/docs/local-ci-runner).

## Turn on a ready-made automation

**Workflows → New workflow** opens on a gallery. An empty Workflows tab shows the same cards.

| Automation | When it runs | What it needs |
|---|---|---|
| Summarize my GitHub notifications every morning | Weekdays at a time you pick | GitHub connected, the `gh` CLI signed in, a default model |
| Review every PR I open | Each pull request you open in a repo you pick (checked every 2 minutes) | GitHub connected, the `gh` CLI signed in, a default model |
| Nightly dependency check | Every night at a time you pick | A project folder, a default model |

Each card marks what you already have. Click one to open its setup sheet:

1. **What it needs.** Anything missing has a button: **Connect** opens Connectors, **Choose a
   model** opens Models. A template that runs in a project asks which folder.
2. **Its questions.** A time of day, or a repository (`owner/name`) and your GitHub username.
   Only PRs you open start a review: the trigger checks the event's author and its `opened`
   action exactly, so other people's PRs, reopened PRs and closed ones never reach the agent.
3. **Notify me.** Digests default to *After every run*; change it here or later in the editor.
4. **Turn on.** The automation is created, enabled and armed. The toast says when it runs first.

**Customize** opens the same automation in the workflow editor instead, where you can change its
steps, triggers and model before saving.

Every ready-made automation only reads: it summarizes or reviews, and never comments, posts,
installs or changes anything. Results land in the run history (and a notification, if you asked
for one).

Digests read text other people wrote, such as notification titles or package advisories. So a
fixed command fetches it first, and the agent that summarizes it has **no tools**: it can only
write the summary, so nothing in that text can make it run a command. You can set **No tools** on
any prompt or skill step in the editor. Keep such a step last, because later steps share its
chat and see the same text.

## How a run went

Expand a workflow to see its runs. The selected run shows how long it took and when it started,
then either:

- **Failed at "step"**: the step that failed, its error, and a **Transcript** button for that
  step's chat, or
- **Result**: the last agent step's answer, which for a digest is the digest itself.

The history on the right lists the last ten runs with their status, duration, what started
them, and the step a failed run stopped at.

## Notifications

Each workflow's **Notify me** setting decides when a finished run tells you:

- **When a run fails** (the default, also for workflows made before this setting existed),
- **After every run**, for digests, or
- **Never**.

Clicking a notification opens the Workflows tab on that run. Notifications follow
**Settings → Notifications → Desktop notifications**, and stay quiet while the Workflows tab is on
screen. A run cut short because the app quit is reported as a failure the next time it starts.

Phone notifications for failed runs are not available yet.

## Pause all automations

The **Pause all automations** switch in the Workflows header is the kill switch:

- schedules, pull request and push events, Slack messages, connector polls and webhooks start no
  runs, and scheduled tasks (from a chat's **⚡ Automate** menu) wait;
- whatever is running when you switch it on is stopped;
- the **Run** button, a task's **Run now** and `nekko-agent workflow run` still work.

A schedule that came due while paused runs once when you resume. Events that arrived during the
pause are skipped, not replayed. The setting is shared, so pausing from one window or the web
edition pauses everywhere.

---

<!-- https://nekkoagent.com/docs/local-ci-runner -->

# Local CI runner

Use a machine running Nekko Agent as a CI runner for a GitHub or GitLab repo: when a commit is
pushed or a pull request opens, a workflow checks the code out, runs your build and tests **on
that machine**, and reports the result back to the provider as a commit status - with a comment
on the PR when it fails. It saves hosted-runner minutes by burning your own hardware instead.

## What it is - and what it is not

A "Local CI runner" is a **workflow template**, not a new subsystem. Create it from
**Workflows → New workflow → Local CI runner** (under *Build your own*).
Behind the scenes it is ordinary workflow pieces you already have:

- a **trigger** that fires on repo events (see [Getting events in](#getting-events-in)),
- **shell steps** that check out the commit and run your build/test commands,
- **action steps** (`github.setCommitStatus`, `gitlab.setCommitStatus`, `github.commentPR`,
  `gitlab.commentMR`) that report the outcome back through the saved connector credentials.

**This is not a GitHub Actions self-hosted runner.** Nekko Agent does not speak the
`actions/runner` broker protocol, will not pick up `runs-on: self-hosted` jobs, and does not use
the Checks API (no annotations, no check-suite lifecycle). It produces a plain **commit status**
(`nekko-agent/<workflow>` context) and PR comments - enough for "did this commit pass on my
machine", not a replacement for the Actions job queue. If you need real self-hosted runners, use
GitHub's or GitLab's official runner.

## The template

The workflow looks like this:

```
checkout (shell)  ──fail──▶  report failure (action)  ──▶  comment on PR (action) ──▶ fail
    │
  success
    ▼
build + test (shell) ──success──▶ report success (action) ──▶ end
```

- **Check out the commit** - `git fetch origin {{trigger.branch}} && git checkout {{trigger.sha}}`
- **Build and test** - `npm ci && npm run build && npm test`
- **Report success / failure** - `github.setCommitStatus` with context
  `nekko-agent/<your-workflow-name>` (the default when the `context` param is empty)
- **Comment on the PR** - `github.commentPR` with the tail of the test step's output.
  On plain `push` events there is no PR number, so this step fails and the run still ends red.

**The two shell steps are placeholders.** Edit them for your project - your package manager,
your test command, your merge strategy. The action steps are ready as-is: they take repo, sha,
and PR number from the event when the `{{trigger.*}}` params render empty.

For GitLab, swap the action steps for `gitlab.setCommitStatus` (state `failed`/`success`,
status name `nekko-agent/<workflow>`) and `gitlab.commentMR`.

## Getting events in

A run only happens when an event reaches the workflow. Pick **one** delivery mode per workflow ,
arming two means double runs.

### Poll mode - works anywhere, including the desktop app

The desktop app can't receive real webhooks (it's behind NAT), so the honest default is polling:
Nekko Agent asks the provider's API what's new, on an interval, with a per-trigger cursor stored
in `workflow-cursors.json` next to `workflows.json`.

The template ships a disarmed **Connector** trigger as the starter:

1. Connect GitHub (or GitLab) under **Connectors** - the poller uses that token.
2. On the workflow's Connector trigger: set **Repo** to `owner/name`, set the event name, arm it.
   - GitHub event names are the API's `type` strings: `PushEvent`, `PullRequestEvent`,
     `PullRequestReviewEvent`, … One trigger matches one name, so add a second trigger for PRs.
   - GitLab polls the project events feed; filter with the **Filter** substring field.
3. **Poll every N minutes** defaults to 1. Each new matching event starts a run; a late or
   duplicated page can't refire (events are deduped by id, and the cursor survives restarts).

Polling is eventually-consistent by design: expect up to a poll interval of latency, and note
that repo events APIs are shallow (recent events only).

### Webhook mode - server / Docker edition

When Nekko Agent runs somewhere a provider can reach (the server edition, Docker, a VM with a
public URL), inbound webhooks give instant triggers:

```
POST https://<your-host>/api/hooks/<workflow-slug>?key=<trigger secret>
```

The template ships a disarmed **Webhook** trigger with a generated secret. Arm it, copy the URL
shown in the editor, and add it as a webhook on the repo (GitHub: repo → Settings → Webhooks,
content type `application/json`; GitLab: project → Settings → Webhooks).

- The secret is **per trigger** and travels in `?key=` (or you can relay it). It's compared in
  constant time and never logged. Regenerate it in the editor if it leaks.
- The route enforces a 10 MB body cap and a 60-requests/minute limit per slug+IP.
- The raw provider JSON body becomes the event payload - the action steps understand the common
  shapes (`repository.full_name`, `pull_request.head.sha`, `object_attributes.iid`, …), so the
  template's status/comment steps work without a normalizing layer.
- A `webhook` trigger fires on *any* authenticated POST. Use the trigger's **Filter** field, or
  the git trigger below, if you want to restrict which deliveries start a run.

**Desktop opt-in:** the desktop app can expose the same route on loopback ,
Settings → Experimental → workflow loopback listener binds `127.0.0.1:1441` only. Useful for
local relays and tunnels, off by default.

### Dispatching git events directly - `workflow:event`

The `git` trigger (the one the template ships armed) matches **normalized** events - provider,
event name, repo, branch - dispatched through the generic event door. On the server edition:

```
POST https://<your-host>/api/workflow:event
Authorization: Bearer <NEKKO_TOKEN>
{ "args": [{
    "kind": "git", "provider": "github", "event": "pr_opened",
    "repo": "owner/name", "branch": "feature-x",
    "payload": { "sha": "abc123…", "number": 12 }
}] }
```

This is the door a relay script uses when it sits between a provider webhook and a machine that
can't be reached directly: accept the webhook, map it onto the normalized shape, POST it on.
Inside the desktop app the same call goes over the internal API (`workflow:event`).

## The payload contract

Steps read the event through `{{trigger.*}}` templates (`repo`, `branch`, plus every payload
key) and the action steps fall back to the event when a param renders empty. These keys are
understood - normalized names first, then the raw provider body:

| Need | Normalized | Raw GitHub body | Raw GitLab body |
|---|---|---|---|
| Repo / project | `repo` | `repository.full_name` | `project.path_with_namespace`, `project_id` |
| Commit SHA | `sha` | `after`, `head_commit.id`, `pull_request.head.sha`, `head` | `checkout_sha`, `object_attributes.last_commit.id` |
| PR / MR number | `number`, `pull_number` | `number`, `pull_request.number`, `issue.number` | `iid`, `object_attributes.iid` |
| Branch | `branch` | `ref` (`refs/heads/…`) | `ref` |

Reported statuses use context `nekko-agent/<workflow-slug>` on GitHub (states
`success`/`failure`/`error`/`pending`) and the same name on GitLab (`success`/`failed`/
`running`/`pending`/`canceled`) - each op accepts the other's spelling for `state`.

## Security model, honestly stated

| Threat | Defense |
|---|---|
| A stranger's PR runs code on your machine | **None by default - this is the big one.** Shell steps run unattended, as you, in the workflow's workspace. Only point this at repos you control, or gate it (see below). |
| Webhook spoofing | Per-trigger secret in `?key=`, constant-time compare, 60 req/min rate limit, 10 MB body cap |
| Exposed endpoint | Server edition binds `127.0.0.1` by default; the desktop listener is loopback-only and off unless enabled |
| Credential theft via the workflow | Connector tokens live in settings, never on the step; a workflow file carries no secrets except its webhook keys |
| Event injects a shell command | The command line comes from your workflow, not the event - but `{{trigger.*}}` values are interpolated *before* exec, so only interpolate fields you trust (git SHAs and ref names can't contain shell metacharacters; a free-text payload field can) |

**Untrusted pull requests need review.** Anyone who can open a PR against your repo could get
their code executed on this machine. Guardrails that actually help:

- Restrict the trigger's **Repo** and **Branches** (e.g. `main`, `release/*`) so random forks
  and branches don't fire it.
- Prefer the git trigger with an explicit event list over a wide-open webhook trigger.
- For public repos, keep the runner on a dedicated workspace you don't mind being compromised,
  or add a `prompt` step that reviews the diff before the shell steps run.
- One run per workflow at a time: events that arrive while a run is in flight are skipped, not
  queued - so a push flood can't stack runs, but it can also drop builds.

## Limits

- Local execution only: runs happen on the machine hosting Nekko Agent, with its CPU, its
  toolchain, and its uptime. A closed laptop is a runner that's down.
- Shell steps time out after 600s by default (`timeoutSec` per step); step output kept in the
  run log is trimmed to ~4 KB.
- No parallelism beyond one run per workflow, no job matrix, no artifacts - it's a
  workflow engine, not a CI fleet.

---

<!-- https://nekkoagent.com/docs/decision-models -->

# Decision models

A decision model answers typed questions about a piece of text with calibrated probabilities, in one forward pass, without generating any text. Nekko Agent runs one natively in its engine daemon: **Laya**, an open-weight model from Convai Innovations (Apache 2.0).

## What Laya and Jev are

TypeSafe Jev is a closed, hosted "System One" decision API: you send a `state` (text or JSON) and named questions, and get back typed answers. [Laya](https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya) is an open-weight model trained for the same job, and its own server (`laya-serve`) speaks Jev's request and response shape. Nekko Agent speaks it too, so a Jev client works against the local engine by changing its base URL.

Three question types:

| type | `criteria` | answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `choice` | an object of label -> description, or a list of labels | `{ "type": "choice", "choice": "billing", "confidence": 0.86, "probabilities": { "billing": 0.97, ... } }` |
| `score` | the ordered list of levels, index 0 first | `{ "type": "score", "score": 1.44, "confidence": 0.14, "legend": { "0": "not urgent", ... }, "probabilities": { "0": 0.12, ... } }` |
| `noul` | optional `{ "true": ..., "false": ... }` descriptions | `{ "type": "noul", "noul": 0.82 }` (the probability it is true) |

Every answer also carries Laya's two extras, `answer_confidence` (the top probability, which is what the temperatures are fitted on) and `action.act_probability` (the act/escalate head, which Laya's own README says carries no usable signal yet). The response has `model`, `answers`, `usage` (`input_tokens`, `output_tokens: 0`, and how much of the state was cut to fit), and `latency_ms`.

## The local runtime

`crates/nekko-decide`, inside `nekkod`. No Python at run time: the checkpoint is an ONNX export run by ONNX Runtime (the `ort` crate with prebuilt binaries), and the tokenizer is the checkpoint's `tokenizer.json` (the `tokenizers` crate).

- **Same input as the reference, token for token.** Prompt construction, option markers, the 48-token per-option cap and the head budget, state truncation (from the back for a conversation list, so the newest turn survives), the Python `json.dumps` rendering of JSON states and structured criteria, and temperature clamping all follow the `laya` package (0.3.22). The golden test checks every question's token sequence against the package's own.
- **One call, all questions.** A bad question becomes that question's `error` entry; the others are still answered. Request caps are `laya-serve`'s: 64 questions, 50,000 state characters, 100 options per choice, 32 score levels, 512 options in all.
- **Execution providers.** DirectML on Windows, CoreML on macOS, CUDA on Linux only in a build made with `--features cuda` against a CUDA build of ONNX Runtime (not the release builds; see "CUDA on Linux" below), and CPU everywhere. Each accelerator gets a probe batch at load; one that cannot build or run the graph falls back to CPU at load time, and `decide:status` reports the provider actually in use and why any were skipped.
- **Fixed shapes on DirectML and CoreML.** DirectML only runs fast on a shape it compiled when the session was created: a dynamic session answered its first-seen shape in 15 ms and every other shape in about 85 ms. Accelerated sessions therefore pin one row of `max_len` tokens and 128 option slots, and run a call's questions one after another. CPU and CUDA batch every question of a call in one run.
- **Surfaces.** Daemon channels `decide:load` (`[dir, precision?]` or `[{ dir, precision?, ep?, name? }]`), `decide:unload`, `decide:status` and `decide:run` (`[{ model?, state, questions }]`); on the engine's OpenAI-compatible port, `POST /v1/decisions` (Jev's path) and `POST /v1/systemone` (`laya-serve`'s), behind the same API key and CORS as every other route, answering 409 when no decision model is loaded.
- **Model directory.** `model_fp16.onnx` (default), `model.onnx` (fp32, may have a `.data` file beside it) or `model_int8.onnx`, plus `tokenizer.json` (at the root or under `tokenizer/`) and `rl_agent_config.json`.

## Measured

RTX 5090, Ryzen 9 9950X3D, Windows 11, release build, the English checkpoint, the README's support-ticket email as the state (`cargo run --release -p nekko-decide --example latency -- <dir> <ep> <precision>`). p50 of 100 (DirectML) or 10 (CPU) calls after warm-up:

| | 1 question | 10 questions | load |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DirectML, fp16 | **8.6 ms** | 81 ms | 1.5-2.7 s |
| DirectML, fp32 | 15 ms | 154 ms | 2.5 s |
| DirectML, fp16, dynamic shapes (not used) | 86 ms | 102 ms | |
| CPU, fp32 | 94 ms | 733 ms | 3.7 s |
| CPU, fp16 | 106 ms | 707 ms | 2.5 s |
| CPU, int8 | 68 ms | 731 ms | 1.0 s |

Laya's README reports 39.5 ms and 158.6 ms on a T4 with torch. Batching ten questions into one DirectML run would be faster than ten runs of one, but only with a second fixed-shape session, which doubles GPU memory; not done.

The same machine and model files, measured again on 2026-10-17 for every checkpoint (p50 of 100 calls; CUDA in Docker under WSL2 on the same GPU, `scripts/decision-models/cuda-golden.sh`; Linux CPU in the same container):

| | laya-en, 1 / 10 questions | laya-multilingual | laya-typed-decisions | load (laya-en) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DirectML, fp16 (Windows) | 8.4 / 86 ms | 10.6 / 106 ms | 17.4 / 175 ms | 1.4 s |
| DirectML, fp32 (Windows) | 15.6 / 155 ms | | | 1.9 s |
| CUDA, fp16 (Linux) | 10.5 / 13.3 ms | 8.0 / 9.1 ms | 10.9 / 13.2 ms | 5.3 s |
| CUDA, fp32 (Linux) | 10.3 / 20.6 ms | 8.0 / 11.6 ms | 10.3 / 20.6 ms | 10.6 s |
| CPU, fp32 (Windows) | 90 / 787 ms | | | 1.7 s |
| CPU, fp32 (Linux, what Linux release builds run) | 71 / 560 ms | | | 10 s |

CUDA batches a call's questions into one run, so ten questions cost little more than one; DirectML runs them one after another on its fixed shape. The typed-decisions model is slower on DirectML than the English one with the same architecture because its 1,024-token budget is the fixed shape every question is padded to.

### CUDA on Linux (PF33)

`--features cuda` makes `ort` download pyke's ONNX Runtime 1.28 build with CUDA 13. **That build does not run on an RTX 50-series (Blackwell, sm_120) GPU**: its CUDA kernels are compiled for sm_75, sm_80 and sm_90 only and carry no PTX, so every session fails its probe ("CUDA failure 209: no kernel image is available for execution on the device") and the runtime falls back to the CPU, correctly but silently fast-less. Microsoft's own 1.28.3 build (`onnxruntime-linux-x64-gpu_cuda13`, sm_75 to sm_120 plus sm_120 PTX) works when linked dynamically (`ORT_LIB_LOCATION=<its lib> ORT_PREFER_DYNAMIC_LINK=1`); mixing its provider library with pyke's static core does not ("ComputeAsync is not implemented"). With it, all three checkpoints pass the golden test on CUDA (fp32 max error 0.0001, fp16 0.017 / 0.020 / 0.006, every answer the same). ONNX Runtime's CUDA provider runs fp32 MatMuls in TF32 by default, which moved fp32 probabilities by up to 0.004; the runtime now turns TF32 off.

**Decision: Linux release builds do not ship CUDA.** What shipping it would take: Microsoft's `libonnxruntime.so` (27 MB) and CUDA provider (267 MB) beside `nekkod`, 295 MB on top of a 203 MB AppImage and 157 MB .deb, plus a CUDA 13 runtime and cuDNN 9 that are not on most Linux machines and are over 1 GB to bundle. What it buys: about 60 ms per question (71 to 10 ms) and 0.5 s per ten-question call. Decision calls are agent tool calls next to chat-model turns that take seconds, so the CPU is fast enough, and Windows (DirectML) and Macs (CoreML) already get the GPU without any of this. Revisit if Linux users ask for it; the way to do it would be a separately downloaded runtime (as DirectML.dll is fetched on demand) rather than a bigger package. Self-builders can use the commands in `scripts/decision-models/cuda-golden.sh`.

### CoreML on macOS

`.github/workflows/decision-models.yml` (run by hand, and on changes to `crates/nekko-decide`) downloads the exports, checks their SHA-256 sums, and runs the golden test with CoreML requested on a `macos-14` (Apple silicon) runner, writing which provider actually ran each checkpoint to the job summary. GitHub's macOS runners are virtual machines without the Neural Engine, and Apple's paravirtualized GPU may or may not take the model, so a CPU fallback there does not prove one on a real Mac, while a CoreML pass proves the graph compiles and answers correctly under CoreML. The first run (2026-10-17) did not get that far: the golden set under CoreML on the VM was still running when the job hit its 60-minute limit, so it showed neither a CoreML run nor a fallback. The workflow now asks the latency example first, which reports the provider in use and any fallback reason within minutes. Its second run (2026-10-17, laya-en fp16 on `macos-14`) answered: **CoreML took the model, with no fallback**, but it is unusably slow in the VM: load 127 s, one question 32.8 s p50 (39.7 s p95, 5 runs), against about 0.07 s on a CPU, and the ten-question call did not finish inside the step's 30 minutes. The runner's GPU is paravirtualized and it has no Neural Engine, so this says nothing yet about a real Mac, but if a real Mac is anywhere near this slow, CoreML must not be the default there (`Ep::accelerators()` would need to prefer the CPU on macOS). That is what the Mac check below decides.

**Checking CoreML on a Mac** (Apple silicon, about 3 GB of disk and 10 minutes): with Rust and the GitHub CLI installed, from a checkout of this repository run

```sh
bash scripts/decision-models/mac-check.sh            # laya-en
bash scripts/decision-models/mac-check.sh laya-en laya-multilingual laya-typed-decisions
rm -rf ~/nekko-decision-check                       # afterwards
```

It downloads the exports (checked against `SHA256SUMS`), runs the golden test with CoreML requested and on the CPU in fp16 and fp32, and the latency example, then prints a summary. What to look for: each line says `on coreml` (CoreML ran it) or `on cpu` (it fell back; the latency run above prints the reason), the token check says 86, the answers say 86/86, and the max error stays under 0.02 for fp16 and 0.001 for fp32. Paste the summary and the latency lines into the PR or TASKS.md (PF33).

## Accuracy against the reference

`crates/nekko-decide/tests/golden/` holds 60 requests (86 questions: all three types, 1 to 30 options, states from empty to far past the 512-token window, JSON and conversation states, unicode, structured criteria, `option_order`) and what the official `laya` 0.3.22 package answered on CPU in fp32, once per checkpoint (`golden.json` for English, `golden-multilingual.json`, `golden-typed-decisions.json`; `LAYA_GOLDEN` picks one). The test runs when `LAYA_MODEL_DIR` points at a model directory and is skipped otherwise, so CI never downloads the model. Every row below has every token sequence identical to the reference's (86/86).

Measured on the hosted files (`decision-models-v1`), RTX 5090, Windows (DirectML, CPU) and Linux in Docker (CUDA). Max and mean absolute probability error; answers the same as the reference's:

| | laya-en | laya-multilingual | laya-typed-decisions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| fp32, CPU | 0.0001 / 0.00002, 86/86 | 0.0000 / 0.00002, 86/86 | 0.0000 / 0.00003, 86/86 |
| fp32, DirectML | 0.0001 / 0.00002, 86/86 | 0.0001 / 0.00002, 86/86 | 0.0000 / 0.00003, 86/86 |
| fp16, DirectML | 0.0186 / 0.00097, 86/86 | 0.0157 / 0.00080, 86/86 | 0.0057 / 0.00057, 86/86 |
| fp16, CPU | 0.0173 / 0.00049, 86/86 | 0.0029 / 0.00016, 86/86 | 0.0053 / 0.00036, 86/86 |
| int8, CPU | 0.048 / 0.0037, 86/86 | 0.125 / 0.0068, 85/86 | 0.025 / 0.0023, 85/86 |
| fp32, CUDA (Linux) | 0.0000 / 0.00002, 86/86 | 0.0001 / 0.00002, 86/86 | 0.0000 / 0.00003, 86/86 |
| fp16, CUDA (Linux) | 0.0167 / 0.00058, 86/86 | 0.0196 / 0.00076, 86/86 | 0.0060 / 0.00039, 86/86 |

The test fails fp32 over 1e-3, fp16 over 0.02 and int8 over 0.06, and fp32 or fp16 on any changed answer. That means the multilingual int8 file fails it (one answer flips, a 0.125 move on a 15-option near-tie): its 256k-token embedding table is a Gather, which the weight-only quantizer leaves in fp32, so the file is larger than fp16 (929 MB against 646 MB) and less accurate. It is on the release for completeness but not in the app's catalog. The typed-decisions int8 flip is a near-tie on a 14-option question and inside int8's bound.

## The hosted export

The app downloads the exports from a release of this repository, [`decision-models-v1`](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/releases/tag/decision-models-v1). It is never marked the latest release, because the app's updater (`crates/nekkod/src/native.rs`) and the website read `releases/latest`. Assets are named `<checkpoint>.<file>`; `SHA256SUMS` lists all of them, `LICENSE` is upstream's Apache-2.0 license and `NOTICE` says what was changed. The catalog (`DECISION_CATALOG` in `packages/host/src/engine/decisions.ts`, mirrored by the daemon through its golden file) pins every file's size and SHA-256.

| checkpoint | upstream (pinned) | fp16 | fp32 | int8 | tokenizer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `laya-en` | `convaiinnovations/laya@55cf4c4` | 846 MB | 1,689 MB | 612 MB | 3.6 MB |
| `laya-multilingual` | `convaiinnovations/laya-multilingual@e4e9ddf` | 646 MB | 1,290 MB | 929 MB (not offered) | 34 MB |
| `laya-typed-decisions` | `convaiinnovations/laya-typed-decisions@1a793eb` | 846 MB | 1,689 MB | 612 MB | 3.6 MB |

The revisions are the ones laya 0.3.22 itself pins as reviewed (`laya.revisions.PINNED_REVISIONS`); their weights are byte-identical to `main` today. Upstream's license is Apache-2.0 (the GitHub repository's `LICENSE`, and every checkpoint's model card), which allows redistributing the weights and derivative works with the license and a notice of changes; upstream ships no NOTICE file of its own.

**Download in the app.** Nekko Server's Decisions tab lists all three. Downloading one precision queues its four small files and the model file as one group in the engine daemon's download queue (`decisions:download`, `crates/nekkod/src/decisions.rs`, the same queue as chat models: resumable, cancellable, shown in Downloads). Each file is checked against its published size and SHA-256 before it is renamed into place, so a file that is not the published one is refused and deleted, never loaded; a file already on disk at its published size is kept. Measured: laya-en fp16 (0.85 GB) from the real release into an empty data directory in 62 s, loaded on DirectML fp16 in 2.2 s, and the README's support email answered `billing` (0.988) in 19 ms (`scripts/itest-decision-download.mjs`).

## The export recipe

`scripts/decision-models/` rebuilds every hosted file from the pinned checkpoints (README there). Python is used at build time only, in a throwaway virtual environment.

1. fp32: laya's own `scripts/export_onnx.py` recipe (torch dynamo exporter, opset 18, dynamic batch, sequence and option counts, traced from batch-2 dummies).
2. Clear `allowzero` on every `Reshape` (DirectML refuses `allowzero=1`; no shape tensor in this graph holds a literal 0, so the result is identical).
3. fp16: `onnxruntime.transformers.float16.convert_float_to_float16(model, keep_io_types=True)` after deleting the graph's `value_info` (stale intermediate types are what broke the tozp file). For laya-en and laya-typed-decisions the rotary-embedding angle nodes (`Cos`/`Sin` and what feeds them, 14 small nodes) stay in fp32: the angles reach ~500 rad at 512 tokens, where fp16 resolves only 0.25 rad, and plain fp16 put laya-en at 0.0213 on DirectML, just over the test's 0.02. The multilingual model measured better plain (0.0157 against 0.0343), so it is converted plain. Keeping nodes in fp32 makes the converter insert duplicate Casts out of order; the script drops the duplicates and sorts the graph.
4. int8: weight-only, `MatMulNBitsQuantizer` with 8 bits, block size 128, symmetric, `accuracy_level=4`. Laya's own recipe (`quantize_dynamic`) quantizes activations per tensor and moves logits by up to 3.7 on the English checkpoint, flipping 20 of 86 answers.
5. The tokenizer and config files are upstream's own bytes, fetched fresh (loading laya rewrites the cached `tokenizer_config.json` of the multilingual checkpoint in place).

`reference.py` regenerates the golden files; rerun on the English checkpoint it reproduces the committed `golden.json` (identical tokens, probabilities within 4e-6, from torch 2.14.0 to 2.14.1).

The only other public export, `tozp/laya-onnx`, was traced with TorchScript at opset 14 from a batch-1, 512-token dummy input: its decision head only runs at exactly 512 tokens, and at 512 its logits are off by up to 4 against the reference (36 of 86 golden answers match). Its fp16 file also fails to load on ONNX Runtime's CPU provider (a type error in a converter-inserted Cast, and an access violation with full optimizations). The runtime refuses exports below opset 17 with a message saying why, since that CPU failure would otherwise take the daemon down.

## Limitations and open items

- **No automatic routing between checkpoints.** laya's `Router` picks the multilingual checkpoint for non-Latin scripts; here the user picks the model they load, and one is loaded at a time. `laya-multilingual` runs at its shipped 1,024-token budget (the 8,192-token mode is not offered).
- **The model's own limits.** The English checkpoint is near chance on the typed-decisions benchmark zero-shot, ships over-confident (the `choice:11+` temperature is clamped from 0.10 to 0.5, as laya does, and those confidences are uncalibrated), and many options share a 192-token head budget, so questions with dozens of options lose accuracy. See Laya's README, "Honest Limits".
- **Not verified here:** CoreML on a real Mac (the checklist above is for that; it falls back to the CPU if it fails), and a DirectML machine older than this one. CUDA is verified on Linux in Docker on an RTX 5090, with Microsoft's ONNX Runtime build.
- **Windows runtime libraries.** ONNX Runtime is statically linked, and on Windows it makes `nekkod` import the Visual C++ runtime's `MSVCP140.dll` (Rust already needed `VCRUNTIME140.dll` from the same package). pyke's prebuilt ONNX Runtime is compiled against the DLL runtime (`/MD`), so `nekkod` cannot link the runtime statically; instead the installer and the npm package ship the runtime DLLs app-local beside `nekkod` (`scripts/vc-runtime.mjs`), and a PC without the Visual C++ Redistributable still starts it.
- **DirectML is not shipped.** `nekkod` delay-loads `DirectML.dll` (`crates/nekkod/build.rs`), and before the DirectML provider starts `crates/nekko-decide/src/directml.rs` loads a copy at least 1.15: Windows' own `System32\DirectML.dll` (Windows 11 has carried one since 2024), or one the host fetched. On a Windows whose copy is older (Windows 10), loading a model fetches Microsoft's `DirectML.dll` 1.15.4 once, reading only that entry out of the `Microsoft.AI.DirectML` NuGet package with HTTP range requests (about 9 MB of a 200 MB package) and checking it against a pinned SHA-256 (`packages/host/src/engine/directml.ts`). If that fails the model loads on the CPU and the load message says why. This took 18 MB off every install.

---

<!-- https://nekkoagent.com/docs/benchmarks -->

# Local inference benchmarks

How fast Nekko Agent's engine runs a model compared with Ollama and LM Studio, on the same machine and the same model file, measured the same way. vLLM is supported by the harness but not measured here (it has no native Windows build).

The numbers are from one machine. They are not a promise about yours; run the harness (below) to get your own.

## Results, 2026-09-30

**Model:** `gemma-4-12B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf` (lmstudio-community), the same file for every server. **Machine:** NVIDIA RTX 5090 32 GB, AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D, Windows 11. Median of 3 runs; 32k context; everything on the GPU.

| Measure | Nekko Agent engine | llama.cpp as the engine ran it before | Ollama 0.23.0 | LM Studio (llama.cpp CUDA 12, 2.46.0) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Decode, tokens/s | **154** | 127 | 115 | 116 |
| Code edit that repeats its input, tokens/s | **534** | 117 | 106 | 108 |
| Four requests at once, total tokens/s | **256** | 283 | 113 | 210 |
| Time to first token, short prompt | **99 ms** | 98 ms | 153 ms | 114 ms |
| Prefill of an 8k-token prompt, tokens/s | 5,832 | 5,968 | **6,170** | 5,886 |
| New agent session (8k-token context), first turn to first token | 1,719 ms | 2,280 ms | **1,280 ms** | 2,565 ms |
| Agent session, later turns to first token | 253 ms | 219 ms | **211 ms** | 288 ms |
| Agent session, six turns end to end | 7.9 s | 8.4 s | **7.6 s** | 9.3 s |

Six chats visited in turn, three rounds each, more chats than the server has slots (what a person with several agent chats open does):

| | Nekko Agent engine | llama.cpp default prompt cache | llama.cpp, no RAM prompt cache | Ollama | LM Studio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Revisit of a chat, to first token | **790 ms** | 1,729 ms | 1,894 ms | 1,290 ms | 1,600 ms |
| All three rounds, end to end | **27.1 s** | 32.0 s | 38.4 s | 31.7 s | 33.3 s |

### Reading the results honestly

- **Where Nekko Agent is clearly ahead:** edits that repeat their input (about 4.5x the other servers, from n-gram speculative decoding), plain decode (about a third faster), coming back to a chat that lost its slot (about 40% faster than Ollama), and parallel requests (Ollama serves one at a time by default).
- **Where it is not:** the first turn of a brand-new long conversation is slower than Ollama's (1.7 s against 1.3 s), and prefill is level with everyone. The first-turn gap was 2.3 s before this work; the remaining difference is under investigation.
- **Noise:** run-to-run variation was about 10% on prefill and larger on the four-request number (the same configuration measured 256, 283 and 343 tokens/s across runs). Differences smaller than that are not claims.
- "Nekko Agent engine" here is `llama-server` from the pinned llama.cpp build started with exactly the flags the engine now passes, measured without the engine's router in front of it. The router (Rust, in the engine daemon) adds about 0.1 ms per request: 27.39 ms against 27.29 ms straight to the model server, median of 30 one-token requests.

### What changed to get there

Measured flag by flag on the same model and build (b11011):

- **`--spec-default`** (n-gram speculative decoding from the conversation, no draft model): code edit 117 to 506-534 tokens/s, decode 127 to 154-155.
- **`--no-cache-idle-slots`**: llama.cpp's default copies every idle slot to its RAM prompt cache when a new request arrives. Keeping them in place cut the first turn of a new chat from 2.3 s to 1.7 s and a revisit of an evicted chat from 1.7 s to 0.8 s. The RAM cache still catches what a slot really loses (turning it off entirely was worse on both).
- **`--cache-reuse 256`**: reuse cached chunks around an edit in the middle of a prompt.
- **Vision models keep it.** With Gemma's projector loaded as well, the code edit ran at 633 tokens/s and decode at 152; llama.cpp only drops `--cache-reuse` for multimodal models.
- **A draft model is opt-in, not automatic.** Gemma 4 E4B as the draft for the 12B raised the code edit to 624 tokens/s but halved ordinary decode (155 to 74) because only 55% of its guesses were accepted. A draft helps only when it is much smaller than its target.
- Parallel slots and a shared KV pool were already llama.cpp's default (`-np` auto with a unified cache), so nothing changed there.

Each flag is passed only when the installed engine build supports it (the engine reads the binary's `--help` once), so an older engine keeps working without them.

## Reproducing

The harness is `crates/nekko-bench`. It measures; it does not start servers.

```bash
cargo build --release -p nekko-bench
```

Start each server with the same GGUF, then list them in a config file:

```json
{
  "machine": "RTX 5090 32 GB, Windows 11",
  "model": "gemma-4-12B-it Q4_K_M",
  "repeats": 3,
  "targets": [
    { "name": "Nekko Agent engine", "baseUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:18095/v1", "model": "gemma" },
    { "name": "Ollama", "baseUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1", "model": "bench-gemma" },
    { "name": "LM Studio", "baseUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1", "model": "bench-gemma" }
  ]
}
```

```bash
target/release/nekko-bench bench.json --out results.json --markdown results.md
```

`--only decode,agent` runs a subset. The workloads: `decode`, `prefill`, `agent` (six turns over an 8k-token context), `rotate` (six chats, three rounds), `code-edit`, `concurrent` (four at once).

How each server was started for the results above:

- **Nekko Agent engine:** `llama-server --model <gguf> --alias gemma --port 18095 --ctx-size 32768 --n-gpu-layers 999 --cache-reuse 256 --spec-default --no-cache-idle-slots`
- **llama.cpp as before:** the same without the last three flags.
- **Ollama:** a Modelfile with `FROM <gguf>`, `PARAMETER num_ctx 32768`, `PARAMETER num_gpu 999`, then `ollama create bench-gemma -f Modelfile`.
- **LM Studio:** `lms server start` and `lms load google/gemma-4-12b --context-length 32768 --gpu max --identifier bench-gemma`.

The harness counts tokens from each server's usage report when it sends one, and times the first streamed piece of text or reasoning as the first token.

# Contributing to Nekko Agent

Thanks for your interest! Nekko Agent is an open-source, local-first AI coding & cowork desktop app. Contributions of all sizes are welcome.

## Development setup

Requires Node 22.12+ and a Rust toolchain ([rustup.rs](https://rustup.rs)): `npm run dev` and `npm run build` compile the engine daemon (`nekkod`). The project uses **npm workspaces** (not pnpm/yarn).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent
cd nekko-agent
npm install
npm run dev          # build the Rust daemon and the app, then launch the desktop app
```

To stop a dev run, press **Enter** or **q** (or Ctrl+C) in its terminal. The app quits the normal way, stopping the engine and any model servers it started; press again to force it, which ends the whole process tree. A run that hasn't exited after 10 seconds is forced too.

## Project layout

| Path | What |
| --- | --- |
| `packages/shared` | Types + IPC contracts (pure, no runtime deps) |
| `packages/core` | Engine: providers, agent loop, guardrails, context, indexer, memory, connectors. **No Electron imports**, unit-tested with Vitest. |
| `apps/desktop` | Electron app: `src/main` (Node), `src/preload` (bridge), `src/renderer` (React) |
| `apps/website` | Static marketing site |
| `scripts/itest-local.mjs` | Manual end-to-end test against a real model server |

**Rule of thumb:** business logic goes in `packages/core` (so it's testable without Electron); the desktop app wires it to the filesystem, shell, and UI.

## Publishing the `npx nekko-agent` package

`npm run bundle:web` produces a self-contained package in `apps/web-app-server/cli-dist/`
(server + engine bundled by esbuild, plus the built `web/` UI). To release it:

```bash
npm run bundle:web
cd apps/web-app-server/cli-dist && npm publish
```

After that, anyone can run the web edition with `npx nekko-agent`.

## Before you open a PR

Keep the build green and the suite passing:

```bash
npm run build       # Rust daemon (nekkod), then shared → core → host → cli → desktop
npm test            # tests in every workspace (one Vitest run over all of them)
npm run typecheck   # every TypeScript workspace
```

`npm test` runs the root `node --test` scripts, desktop's `test:node`, then a single
`vitest run` whose projects (root `vitest.config.ts`) are the eight workspaces. Narrow it
with `npx vitest run --project packages/core`, or run one package as before with
`npm test -w @nekko-agent/core`.

- Add tests in `packages/core` for new engine behavior (providers, guardrails, agent loop, context).
- Desktop UI flows: add a step to a journey in `apps/desktop/e2e/` (`npm run test:e2e -w @nekko-agent/desktop`, hidden windows only; see its README) rather than a new one-off script.
- Match the surrounding code style; keep changes focused.
- For provider changes, you can verify against a real local server:
  `node scripts/itest-local.mjs http://your-host:port your-model-id`

## Documentation

The docs at [nekkoagent.com/docs](https://nekkoagent.com/docs) are rendered from Markdown in this repo. `docs/hub/nav.json` lists the pages and the file each comes from. After editing one of those files, regenerate the site and commit the result with your change. When a pull request changes what users see or do, update the page that describes it in the same PR.

```bash
npm run docs
```

To look at the result before it ships, `npm run website` serves the site on [http://127.0.0.1:8080](http://127.0.0.1:8080) (set `PORT` to change it), with the same clean URLs as production.

If you forget, the **Docs site** workflow regenerates the pages on your pull request and pushes them to its branch. It only commits when something actually changed.

## Commit messages

Conventional commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `chore:`).

## Reporting bugs / requesting features

Use the issue templates. For local-model issues, please include your provider
kind (Ollama / LM Studio / vLLM / cloud), the base URL shape, and the model id.

## License

By contributing, you agree your contributions are licensed under the [MIT License](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/blob/main/LICENSE).

<!-- https://nekkoagent.com/docs/architecture -->

# Architecture

Nekko Agent is one engine and one React UI that run in several places: the desktop app, the self-hosted web edition, Docker and the phone. This page is a map of the code for contributors. The full technical plan, with every decision and task, is in [`TASKS.md`](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/blob/main/TASKS.md); what the product does and why is in [`SPEC.md`](https://github.com/nekko-labs/nekko-agent/blob/main/SPEC.md).

## The big picture

```text
 desktop window (Electron + React)        browser (web edition, Docker)
            |                                        |
            |  IPC                          HTTP + WebSocket
            v                                        v
       apps/desktop main                  apps/web-app-server
            \                                        /
             \----------- nekkod (Rust) ------------/
                     engine daemon on loopback
                    /            |              \
          native services   model servers   TS host (packages/host)
          (chat, tools,     (llama-server,   for everything not
           terminals, ...)   routed)          ported to Rust yet
```

- **The UI never shares a process with the agent.** The window talks to `nekkod`, the engine daemon, over a loopback connection with a per-launch token. The agent loop, terminals and model servers run there, so a busy agent cannot freeze the interface.
- **The engine is moving from TypeScript to Rust.** `nekkod` answers what has been ported natively and passes the rest to the TypeScript host it supervises. Each ported piece has to match the TypeScript behaviour exactly before it takes over.
- **Every edition is the same app.** Desktop, web and Docker run the same engine and the same UI. Only the transport differs: Electron IPC on the desktop, HTTP and WebSocket in the browser.

## Desktop lifetime and notifications

Closing the UI already hides it to the tray without stopping the engine. Explicit Quit shuts down the service and managed processes; Stop Nekko service stops the engine without quitting the UI. Neither arrangement promises continued work during OS sleep, shutdown or logout.

The 2026-10-13 implementation moves Electron native notifications into main (`apps/desktop/src/main/notifications.ts`), with a direct authenticated engine WebSocket subscription, fresh settings reads per eligible notice, reconnect/backoff and disposal on Quit. Main creates native notices; click delivery uses an encoded session deep link to restore the window and select the chat. Renderer notifications remain for browser editions only, avoiding duplicate Electron delivery. Settings exposes the default-on toggle in its standalone Notifications section.

TS host and Rust usage summaries emit matching per-day session costs, local tokens, avoided costs and model ids. Budget aggregates those UTC buckets for every recorded detail instead of mixing a range with lifetime totals. Utilization's same-token Claude dedupe is display-only and prefers Anthropic, without changing provider routing or storage.

Status: implemented, unit and isolated fixture interaction tested; image/motion inspection and native toast delivery/click/permissions testing pending. Main currently assumes events are unattended, so focused-visible-chat suppression is a known review issue. Parent owns resolution and landing.

## Repository layout

| Path | What lives there |
| --- | --- |
| `packages/shared` | Types and IPC contracts. Pure, no runtime dependencies. |
| `packages/core` | The TypeScript engine: providers, agent loop, guardrails, context, indexer, memory, connectors. No Electron imports, unit tested with Vitest. |
| `packages/host` | Wires the engine to the file system, shell and settings. Shared by every edition. |
| `apps/desktop` | The Electron app: `src/main` (Node), `src/preload` (the bridge) and `src/renderer` (React). |
| `apps/web-app-server` | The self-hosted web edition, also the `npx nekko-agent-web` package. |
| `apps/cli` | The `nekko-agent` CLI and MCP server. |
| `apps/mobile` | The iOS and Android app (Expo). |
| `apps/relay` | The relay that pairs a phone with a computer. It only ever sees encrypted frames. |
| `apps/cloud` | Nekko Agent Cloud, the planned hosted edition. |
| `apps/website` | nekkoagent.com, including these docs. |
| `crates/nekkod` | The engine daemon. |
| `crates/nekko-*` | The daemon's services: chat turns, tools, terminals, inference, remote access, storage, usage and more. |

## Build order

`npm run build` builds the Rust daemon, then the TypeScript workspaces in dependency order: `shared`, `core`, `host`, `cli`, `desktop`. `npm run dev` runs a faster variant (the daemon in the incremental `dev-daemon` profile, no production desktop bundle, since electron-vite dev builds its own) and launches the desktop app.

## Where to put new code

- Engine behaviour goes in `packages/core` or a Rust crate, so it can be tested without Electron.
- The desktop app only wires the engine to the window, the file system and the shell.
- A change to what the product does also updates `SPEC.md`; a change to how it is built updates `TASKS.md`.
